routes.reason: ML.2, the potential automorphy assembly, owns the paper's two final theorems and every step of their proof that uses the Dwork family together with automorphy: 'Apply PotentialAutomorphyInfrastructure with full regularity, polarization, residual-image, local and field-extension hypotheses; track compatible systems and descent. Supply the final theorem'. It takes Theorem 1.1 (item 009) and Theorem 1.4 (item 010, with the hypothesis l > n, E2). It also takes the steps of the proof of Theorem 1.1 in §4: the choice of the elliptic curve, of N, of F^avoid and of the auxiliary prime l′ (items 073, 074; E36 adds that l′ must be unramified in F^avoid); the elliptic symmetric-power seed (item 075); the automorphy of the Dwork fibre at l′ (item 082); the passage of automorphy from l′ to l (item 083, with E40); and the Steinberg argument of Lemma 4.3 and Remark 4.4 (items 086–088 and 090, with E1, E41, E43 and E45). Items 073 and 074 come from the Dwork Part II and ArithmeticGaloisRepresentations routes, 075 from ML.3, 083 from PA.5, and 086–088 and 090 from PA.2. Items 073–075 are used by the automorphy of the fibre at l′ (item 082) and by Theorem 1.1, and ML.3, where 075 was, requires ML.2. Items 083, 086–088 and 090 use the Dwork Part II and item 082, and the atlas keeps ModularityAndLanglandsExtensions downstream of PotentialAutomorphyInfrastructure. ML.2 imports: ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 (item 072) from PotentialAutomorphyInfrastructure PA.4; ι-ordinarity, the Steinberg ordinarity criterion and ACC+ Theorem 5.5.1 from PA.2; the base-change lemmas (items 027, 089) from PA.5; Geraghty's Lemma 5.9 (item 133) from the proposed Part II PolarizedAutomorphyLifting; Varma's bound from AutomorphicGaloisRepresentationsPartII AG2.5; Serre's open-image and supersingular theorems (items 137, 138) from the proposed Part II OpenImageTheoremsForAbelianVarieties; and the switching theorem and the Dwork Hodge and monodromy computations from the Dwork Part II. ML.2 currently requires only ML.1 and PA.5, so its blueprint must add PA.2, PA.4 and these Part IIs as prerequisites; none of them depends on ML.2.

G7, the dimension-general arithmetic API, plans the enormous-image definition verbatim (ACC+ Definition 6.2.29) and 'residual-image criteria … with separate verification lemmas'. It covers Lemma 2.6(1) (item 026), which is ACC+ Lemma 7.1.6(2) under the stronger bound l > 2n + 5; the ACC+ extraction places that lemma in G7 as well. The decomposed-genericity lemmas (items 027, 089 and 121) are not here: decomposed genericity is defined at AutomorphicGaloisRepresentationsPartII AG2.7, which requires G7, so G7 cannot state them. They go to PotentialAutomorphyInfrastructure PA.5, which must add AG2.7 as a prerequisite.

R06.2 plans 'D_HT, D_dR, D_cris and D_st and their comparison maps … descent under finite extension, and base change of coefficients … filtered (φ,N)-modules … weak admissibility versus admissibility'. It covers the pointwise definition of an ordinary representation of regular weight (item 002, Definition 1.2, which is word for word condition (2) of ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2), the crystalline slope criterion (item 025, Lemma 2.4 = BLGHT Lemma 2.2(1)), the semistable maximal-monodromy criterion with its Hodge–Tate hypothesis (item 103, BLGHT Lemma 2.2(2), in the form E11 requires), and descent of regular ordinarity (item 104). All four follow from weak admissibility of sub-objects. Item 002 is the single rank-n definition: LocalGaloisDeformationRings L7, which plans ordinary deformation functors, should specialize to it rather than define it again. R06.3 hosts nothing.

PA.2 owns the ordinary tower, 'its commuting positive-monoid operators and the ordinary summand … Track positive monoids, normalization, central characters'. It takes the notion of an ι-ordinary automorphic representation (item 134, Geraghty's Definition 5.3), the resulting notion of an ordinarily automorphic representation (item 005, Definition 1.3), and the general criterion for a twisted Steinberg component to be ι-ordinary (item 135, split out of the proof of Lemma 4.3, generalizing Geraghty's Lemmas 5.2 and 5.6). The Dwork-specific applications of Lemma 4.3 (items 086–088, 090) are in ML.2, since they use the Dwork Part II. The proposed Part II PolarizedAutomorphyLifting, whose brief lists these notions, imports them from here.

ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2, with the hypothesis p > n and the scalar element outside G_{F(ζ_p)} (item 072), is the output of the patching layers of PotentialAutomorphyInfrastructure: ACC+ prove it from Theorem 6.6.2 by soluble base change (§6.6, pp. 1074–1084), using PA.4's Taylor–Wiles primes and ultrapatching, PA.2's ordinary local–global compatibility (Theorem 5.5.1) and PA.5's base-change checklist. It is owned at PA.4; placing it at PA.3, which PA.4 requires, would close a cycle. PA.4 currently requires only PA.3, so its blueprint must add PA.2 and PA.5 as prerequisites; neither depends on PA.4. The ACC+ extraction places Theorems 6.1.1, 6.1.2 and 6.6.2 at PA.3 and should move them with it. ML.2 applies the theorem at p = l′ and p = l.

PA.5 provides 'comparison lemmas for restriction to field extensions, tensor products, duals, characters and symmetric powers' and 'a reusable checklist theorem which records that the input package for a chosen lifting argument survives a specified base change'. It owns the decomposed-genericity lemmas this paper uses: Lemma 2.6(2) (item 027), ACC+ Lemma 7.1.6(3) (item 121), which its proof invokes, the Galois-theoretic lemma on composita with a common simple group (item 122) that the proof also uses, and ACC+ Lemma 7.1.7 (item 089). They need decomposed genericity, which AutomorphicGaloisRepresentationsPartII AG2.7 defines. PA.5 does not yet require AG2.7, so its blueprint must add that dependency; it creates no cycle. The printed proof of Lemma 2.6(2) must apply ACC+ Lemma 7.1.6(3) to the original pair of fields (E22).

R23.1, Moret–Bailly's theorem, plans the rational-point theorem 'with prescribed nonempty local open sets and a finite extension satisfying the required disjointness and real-place conditions', and asks to 'Include the geometric and approximation prerequisites of the theorem'; the description of R23.1 in R24.5:operations adds 'Construct the field-extension selection'. It takes the tower lemma for linear disjointness (item 013; §2 and §4) and the field-selection lemma of Clozel–Harris–Taylor, Lemma 4.1.2 (item 116), which the proof of Lemma 2.1 uses twice (pp. 1245–1246 and p. 1248) and which the proof of Harris–Shepherd-Barron–Taylor, Proposition 2.1, also needs. Proposition 4.2 (item 079) is planned here; its blueprint must state all three kinds of local condition (split places with points in given opens, unramified places, and places with points in Galois-invariant opens over F̄_v), since the paper uses S₁ = {∞} and S₃ = {l, l′}. Lemma 2.1 itself is not a Moret–Bailly statement and is owned by the Dwork Part II.

R02.2 plans 'restriction/corestriction identities and the precise descent consequences for finite extensions of number fields', and R02.4 'the finite-module duality … local invariant maps and their sum'. They cover the general duality statements used in Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2: the inflation identification of the Kummer local–global kernel (item 021), the fact that it is 0 or Z/2Z (item 106), and the computation of H¹ of the cyclotomic Galois group with coefficients μ_{p^r} (item 117, Neukirch–Schmidt–Wingberg Proposition 9.1.6). The locally trivial groups (item 018) and the Poitou–Tate pairing with its Res/Cor adjunction (item 020) are planned at R02.3 and R02.4; the R02.4 blueprint must state the duality for the full absolute Galois group with all places, as p. 1246 uses it. R02.2 must import Chebotarev (Tau Ceti Chebotarev, Layer 10) for item 021. The proof steps of Lemma 2.1 live with that lemma in the Dwork Part II and import these statements.

SF.4 plans 'formal schemes, algebraization, semistable reduction and alterations … a model records its base, generic fiber and allowable base extension'. It owns the general mixed-characteristic toroidal semistable reduction theorem that the companion preprint applies (item 142, Kempf–Knudsen–Mumford–Saint-Donat, Chapters II–IV), with its two inputs, toroidal embeddings over a discrete valuation ring with their subdivision blowups (item 140) and Knudsen's unimodular subdivision after scaling (item 141). Finite fans, cones and subdivisions come from Tau Ceti Analytic toric geometry, Layer 0. The Dwork-specific models (items 091, 092, 094) are in the Dwork Part II, which imports this theorem.

CR.5 plans the log crystalline site and 'the log PD Poincare lemma and its descent', and CR.6 'Construct Frobenius and monodromy N … Construct the Hyodo–Kato-to-log-de-Rham map … Prove its comparison theorem'; the log algebra is the separate stage CR.5:log-algebra. They cover the logarithmic monodromy triangle (item 097) and the N-equivariant comparison of the limit of log-crystalline cohomology of the special fibre with the log de Rham cohomology of a Witt lift over (W, ℕ, 1 ↦ 0) (items 098, 099; companion Theorems 1.6 and 3.2). The CR.6 blueprint must state this comparison in addition to the comparison with the generic fibre, with properness as a hypothesis (E12). Items 098 and 099 hold for any proper log-smooth family over (W[T]′, ℕ, 1 ↦ T) and do not depend on the Dwork model.

Complex Comparison PartII owns coherent GAGA and the algebraic–analytic de Rham comparison: C2 'Construct the cohomology comparison in every degree, naturally in the sheaf', C3 'Export the exact coherent categorical equivalence and cohomology comparison with all properness hypotheses', and C5 the algebraic de Rham complex and its analytification. It takes proper logarithmic GAGA with monodromy (item 100, companion Theorem 1.8), proved by exactly this method, and the local freeness of the relative Hodge filtration of a smooth projective family in characteristic zero (item 130), which Lemma 3.10(2) uses and which no atlas stage plans. The C5 blueprint must state the hypercohomology comparison for bounded complexes of locally free coherent sheaves with differential-operator differentials, with their exact triangles, and must import log differentials from CrystallineCohomology CR.5:log-algebra.

LPV.1 plans 'For a proved unipotent action, define N through the finite logarithm and prove nilpotence' and the monodromy filtration with its linear algebra. It covers maximal unipotence and maximal nilpotence (item 048, Definition 3.6), including dim ker N^j = j. The complex-analytic residue–monodromy theorem (item 101) is not here: LPV.1 is ℓ-adic, and the roadmap supplies 'scheme functors and local calculations, not an automatic comparison for every analytic space' (its README), so it joins the proposed Hodge-structures Part II.

routes.title: Reusable infrastructure for potential automorphy over CM fields, Part II: Dwork switching motives
routes.reason: No layer of the atlas, no draft roadmap and no decomposition plans the Dwork hypersurface family, its eigensheaves, their monodromy or the switching torsor; ModularityAndLanglandsExtensions ML.2, where other extractions send the family, only assembles final theorems. The family is reusable infrastructure for potential automorphy over CM fields: ACC+ Proposition 7.2.3 (pp. 1099–1100) rests on its self-dual version through BLGGT Theorem 3.1.2, Qian's non-self-dual version gives Theorems 1.1 and 1.4, and Qian's n = 2 case is BLGHT's family itself. It is therefore a Part II of PotentialAutomorphyInfrastructure, owning the family once for every exponent vector, together with the lemmas only it uses (Lemma 2.1, the finite-group inputs of Lemma 3.7 and Proposition 3.8, and the companion's semistable models). ML.2 consumes it, and no layer of the parent imports it. Boxer–Calegari–Gee–Newton–Thorne (2025) join this proposal under the same id, parent and title.
routes.brief:
This Part II of Reusable infrastructure for potential automorphy over CM fields builds the Dwork family of hypersurfaces and its cyclotomic eigensheaves. It proves their monodromy, determinant and p-adic Hodge properties, and the switching theorem, which produces a fibre whose residual representations at two primes are prescribed. Nothing here proves an automorphy statement.

Source: L. Qian, Potential automorphy for GL_n, Invent. Math. 231 (2023), 1239–1275, §§2–4. For n = 2 Qian uses the self-dual family of Barnet-Lamb, Geraghty, Harris and Taylor, A family of Calabi–Yau varieties and potential automorphy II, Publ. RIMS 47 (2011), §4 (BLGHT), which is built here too. The companion preprint Qian, Ordinarity of local Galois representation arising from Dwork motives (arXiv:2103.00106v1) supplies the semistable models of the optional last layer.

Where it starts. The parent supplies the cohomological, ordinary, patching and compatible-system infrastructure of Allen et al. (ACC+). It leaves the final potential-automorphy arguments to ModularityAndLanglandsExtensions ML.2, and no layer plans the family those arguments use. This roadmap is its only owner, for every exponent vector. ML.2 imports it; no layer of the parent does.

Setting (pp. 1252–1257). Fix n ≥ 2, an odd prime l, an odd N > 100n + 100 prime to ln, and a CM field F containing ζ_N. Let T_0 = P¹ − ({∞} ∪ μ_N) over Z[1/N], with coordinate t, and let Y ⊂ P^{N−1} × T_0 be the hypersurface X_1^N + ⋯ + X_N^N = N t X_1⋯X_N, smooth and projective over T_0 of relative dimension N − 2. The group H = μ_N^N/μ_N acts by ξ·(X_i, t) = (ξ_i X_i, (∏ξ_i)^{−1} t); its subgroup H_0 = {∏ξ_i = 1}/μ_N acts on every fibre. Construct, once and for an arbitrary exponent vector (a_1, …, a_N) with Σa_i ≡ 0 mod N, the family, the H_0-eigenprojector and the character decomposition of the Fermat fibre, then specialize to Qian's non-self-dual vectors (pp. 1253–1254) and to BLGHT's self-dual vectors with coefficients in Z[1/2N, ζ_N]^+ (E25). B is the set of the n residues b with b + a_j ≢ 0 mod N for every j; V_λ, V[𝔫] and V_B are the χ-eigensheaves of R^{N−2}π_* with coefficients Z[ζ_N]_λ, Z[ζ_N]/𝔫 and Z[ζ_N] (for n = 2, BLGHT's real forms); V′_B is the eigensheaf of the family X_1^N + ⋯ + X_{N−1}^N + t′^{−1}X_N^N = N X_1⋯X_N over T′_0 = P¹ − {0, 1, ∞}, which pulls back to V_B along t′ = t^N.

Final theorems, with the corrections this paper needs.
(1) Lemma 2.3 (p. 1248): given l, s ≥ 1 and a finite set S of primes, there is N prime to l and to S with s | r = ord_N(l) and, when r is even, N ∤ l^{r/2} + 1 (the last display of the proof is a misprint for this, E4).
(2) Lemma 2.1 (p. 1244), built here because only the determinant matching uses it: let M be a CM field, F_0/Q finite Galois, k a finite field of characteristic l, n = l^a m with l ∤ m and m | #k − 1, and χ: G_M → (k^×)^n continuous. Then there are a finite totally real Galois L/Q linearly disjoint from F_0 and ψ: G_{LM} → k^× with ψ^n = χ|G_{LM}. Its proof (the obstruction, the local killing and the two-primary step, items 017 and 022, with E19 and E20) imports the Sha duality and Kummer-kernel statements from ArithmeticGaloisDuality R02.2–R02.4, the low-degree cohomology of Tau Ceti ProfiniteCohomology, the local invariant of Tau Ceti ClassFieldTheory Layer 5, and the field-selection lemma of Clozel–Harris–Taylor from PotentialModularityAndCompatibleSystems R23.1.
(3) Lemma 3.1 (p. 1254): for n > 2, if α ∈ (Z/NZ)^× and αB = B then α = 1.
(4) Proposition 3.2 (p. 1257): V_λ, V[𝔫], V_B and V′_B are locally free of rank n; local freeness needs the torsion-freeness of the middle integral cohomology of smooth hypersurfaces (E24).
(5) Lemmas 3.3–3.4 and Corollary 3.5 (pp. 1257–1259), for n > 2, with loops γ_0γ_1γ_∞ = 1: ρ_{t′}(γ_0) has characteristic polynomial ∏_{b∈B}(X − ζ_N^b); ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) has minimal polynomial (X − 1)^n; ρ_{t′}(γ_1) is a transvection; over C, ρ_{t′} is equivalent to the companion-matrix representation of Beukers–Heckman, by Levelt's theorem (item 123); its reduction modulo a prime of odd residue characteristic prime to N is absolutely irreducible. The printed proof of Lemma 3.3(2) shows only that ρ_{t′}(γ_∞)^N is unipotent (E27): prove (2) through the hypergeometric description (Katz, or the Picard–Fuchs equation with Levelt's theorem). The proof of Lemma 3.3(3) must replace BLGHT's symplectic step by the odd-dimensional Picard–Lefschetz argument or the determinant argument (E28, item 124).
(6) Lemma 3.7 (p. 1259): for n > 2, λ | l, r = ord_N(l) and N ∤ l^{r/2} + 1 when r is even, the residual monodromy of V′_B on T′_0(C) and of V_B on T_0(C) has image SL_n(k(λ)), k(λ) = F_{l^r}. For n = 2 only the statement on T_0(C) holds, by BLGHT Corollary 4.7 (E31: the printed first assertion is false for n = 2). The proof uses Zalesskii–Serezhkin (item 051), the normal subgroups of SL_n over a finite field (item 125) and the finite special unitary groups.
(7) The torsor (pp. 1260–1261): ∧^n V[𝔫] has trivial geometric monodromy and descends to a character of G_F; for W finite free over Z[ζ_N]/𝔫 of rank n with continuous G_F-action and φ: ∧^n W ≅ ∧^n V[𝔫], the isomorphisms ψ: W ≅ V[𝔫] with ∧^n ψ = φ form a finite étale T_W over (T_0)_F. Proposition 3.8: T_W is geometrically connected when 𝔫 = 𝔓_1𝔓_2 with distinct residue characteristics l_1, l_2 prime to 2N (primes of Z[ζ_N]^+ when n = 2, E32), the condition of (6) holds for each l_i when n > 2, and max(l_1, l_2) > 10. The proof needs Artin's theorem that PSL_n over fields of different characteristic are not isomorphic (item 126).
(8) Lemma 3.9 (p. 1262): for λ | l, det V[λ](G_F) ⊂ (F_{l²}^× k(λ)^×)^n, with det(Frob_v | V_{λ,0}) = q^{n(N−n−2)/2}(∏_{b∈B} g(v,b))^n and ∏ g(v,b) ∈ Q_l(ζ_N); for n = 2 the automorphism σ used in the proof need not exist, and any σ in the nontrivial coset works (E33). At the auxiliary prime l′ ≡ 1 mod N, dividing det V_{λ′} by the character with value q^{n(n−1)/2} at geometric Frobenius leaves (q^{(N−2n−1)/2}∏ g(v,b))^n, so its reduction lies in (F_{l′}^×)^n (E6); that character is ε̄^{−n(n−1)/2} (E9).
(9) Lemmas 3.10–3.12 (pp. 1266–1268): the Hodge grades of the Fermat eigenlines, consecutive σ-labelled Hodge–Tate weights M(a), …, M(a) + n − 1; for v | l and t ∈ F_v, as representations of G_{F_v} (E8): V_{λ,t} is de Rham, crystalline when t ∈ O_{F_v} and t^N − 1 is a unit, and ordinary of weight M(a_τ) when l ≡ 1 mod N and t ∈ 𝔪_{F_v}; and, with the hypothesis v(t) < 0 (E1), the monodromy operator of WD(V_{λ′,t}|G_{F_v}) has minimal polynomial X^n.
(10) The switching theorem (§4, pp. 1268–1272), with its data as hypotheses. Let r̄: G_F → GL_n(F_{l^s}) be continuous, F^av/F finite and n = l^a m with l ∤ m. Assume N is as above and prime to the primes ramified in F^av or in F̄^{ker r̄}; k(λ) contains F_{l²} and every m-th root of every element of F_{l^s} (E5); N ∤ l^{r/2} + 1 when r is even; F^avoid is the normal closure over Q of F^av F̄^{ker r̄}(ζ_l); l′ > 2ln + 5 is a prime unramified in F^avoid with l′ ≡ 1 mod N and l′ ≡ 1 mod n (E7, E36); r̄′: G_F → GL_n(F_{l′}) has det r̄′ = ε̄_{l′}^{−n(n−1)/2}; F_2^avoid/Q is finite Galois and F^suff/Q finite totally real Galois, all three avoidance fields unramified above N, F_2^avoid ∩ F^avoid = Q and F^suff ∩ F^avoid F_2^avoid = Q. Then there are a CM field E = L·F(ζ_N) with L/Q totally real Galois and linearly disjoint from F^avoid F_2^avoid F^suff(ζ_N), characters χ_1: G_E → k(λ)^× and χ_2: G_E → F_{l′}^×, a totally real Galois L′/Q and t ∈ T_0(F′) for F′ = L′EF^suff, such that F′/F is CM and Galois, linearly disjoint from F^av, with F′ ∩ F_2^avoid = Q; χ_1^{−1}V[λ]_t ≅ r̄|G_{F′} and χ_2^{−1}V[λ′]_t ≅ r̄′|G_{F′}; v(t) < 0 for every v | l and v(t) > 0 for every v | l′; and L′LF^suff(ζ_N) is linearly disjoint from F^avoid (E3). Lemma 2.1 must be applied twice, enlarging the avoided field before the second application (E37). The proof uses Proposition 3.8 and Moret–Bailly for the Weil restriction of T_W with the local conditions v_l(t_τ) < 0 and v_{l′}(t_τ) > 0.
(11) Optional last layer: the companion's main theorem (item 139) and Remark 3.13, ordinarity of V_{λ,t} for v(t) < 0, proved through the equivariant semistable model (items 091, 092, 094, 143) and BLGHT Lemma 2.2(2), whose Hodge–Tate hypothesis Lemma 3.10(2) supplies; never through the preprint's Lemma 4.2, which omits it (E11). The model gives only potential semistability (E35). Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 do not need this layer.

Built here, since nothing else plans them: Deligne's Fermat computations (Hodge cycles on abelian varieties, §7, Propositions 7.4, 7.6 and 7.10; check the published erratum to that chapter); Levelt's theorem and Beukers–Heckman's irreducibility criterion; BLGHT §4; the argument of Harris–Shepherd-Barron–Taylor Lemma 1.15(2) behind Lemma 3.12; the Zalesskii–Serezhkin classification in the form used (item 051), the normal subgroups of SL_n and Artin's non-isomorphism theorem (items 125, 126), which the maintainer may later move to a finite-group roadmap.

Imports, by title and id: the parent (PotentialAutomorphyInfrastructure); Moret–Bailly's theorem, the field-selection lemma and linear disjointness (PotentialModularityAndCompatibleSystems R23.1); Sha duality and the Kummer kernel (ArithmeticGaloisDuality R02.2, R02.3, R02.4); Isom schemes (AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry R09.2); Weil restriction (ReductiveGroupsPartII RG2.0a); nearby cycles, the local monodromy theorem and Picard–Lefschetz (LefschetzPencilsAndVanishingCycles LPV.0, LPV.1, LPV.2); the Betti–de Rham comparison and the local freeness of the Hodge filtration (ComplexComparisonPartII C3, C5); the residue–monodromy theorem for semistable degenerations (the proposed Hodge structures, Part II: variations, period maps and non-abelian Hodge theory); crystalline, de Rham and semistable comparison (CohomologyComparisons CP.2, CP.3, CP.4); period functors and the ordinarity criteria (PadicHodgeTheory R06.2); log structures and Hyodo–Kato cohomology (CrystallineCohomology CR.5, CR.6); toroidal semistable reduction (SchemeAndStackFoundations SF.4); Gauss and Jacobi sums (FiniteFieldsAndCharacterSums FF.1, with Mathlib's gaussSum); idempotent correspondences and realizations (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles MC.1, MC.2); the pinned Goursat lemma and linear disjointness.

Consumers: ModularityAndLanglandsExtensions ML.2, for Qian's Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 and for the self-dual family behind BLGGT Theorem 3.1.2 and ACC+ Proposition 7.2.3, and Calegari–Geraghty, Invent. Math. 211 (2018), §10. ML.2 keeps the choice of the elliptic curve, of N and of l′, the automorphy of the seed, and the application of the lifting theorem imported from PotentialAutomorphyInfrastructure PA.4, with its hypothesis p > n. Boxer, Calegari, Gee, Newton and Thorne, Forum Math. Pi 13 (2025), §4, join this roadmap with the unitary case, the hypergeometric description and crystalline ordinarity as later layers.

routes.title: Hodge structures (pure, mixed, and polarized), Part II: variations, period maps and non-abelian Hodge theory
routes.reason: The Gauss–Manin residue and analytic monodromy of a semistable degeneration (item 101) is complex-analytic. LefschetzPencilsAndVanishingCycles LPV.1, where the extraction routed it, is ℓ-adic, and that roadmap supplies 'scheme functors and local calculations, not an automatic comparison for every analytic space' (its README), and no atlas stage plans the statement. The proposed Hodge-structures Part II already plans the Deligne canonical extension and its logarithmic de Rham comparison, of which this is the residue computation, so the item joins that proposal under its id, parent, title and area.
routes.brief:
Joined proposal. This route joins HodgeStructuresPartII, the Part II of the Tau Ceti roadmap Hodge structures (pure, mixed, and polarized) proposed by other extractions, with the same id, parent, title and area; its brief already plans the Deligne canonical extension and its logarithmic de Rham complex. Qian's companion preprint (arXiv:2103.00106v1, pp. 21–23) adds one statement, Steenbrink's theorem for semistable degenerations in the logarithmic form of Illusie, Autour du théorème de monodromie locale, Astérisque 223 (1994), Exposé I, 2.2.2 and Corollary 2.2.3.

Setting: S is an open disc with coordinate T and log structure ℕ → O_S, 1 ↦ T, and π: (Y, M) → (S, ℕ) is proper and log smooth of semistable type, smooth over S ∖ {0}, with M the log structure of the reduced normal-crossings fibre over 0. (i) For every i, R^iπ_*ω^•_{(Y,M)/(S,ℕ)} is locally free of finite rank, and its fibre at 0 is H^i of the log de Rham complex of the log special fibre over (pt, ℕ, 1 ↦ 0). (ii) The identification is N-equivariant: on the left N is the residue at 0 of the Gauss–Manin connection, the connecting map of the triangle built from 0 → ω^{•−1}_{Y/S} → ω^•_{Y/C} → ω^•_{Y/S} → 0 by wedge with dlog T; on the right it is the connecting map of the dlog 1 triangle. (iii) On S ∖ {0} the bundle is R^iπ_*C ⊗ O with its Gauss–Manin connection, and the monodromy of R^iπ_*C around 0 is exp(−2πiN) in the source's convention. (iv) Everything commutes with a finite group acting on the family, so it restricts to character eigenspaces, and pulling back along T ↦ T^e replaces the monodromy by its e-th power. The disc must avoid the singular fibres of the algebraic family (E49).

Imports: the Deligne canonical extension and its logarithmic de Rham comparison, already planned in this proposal; the Gauss–Manin connection and coherent GAGA from ComplexComparisonPartII C2, C3, C5, with proper logarithmic GAGA (item 100) there; log structures, log smoothness and log differentials from CrystallineCohomology CR.5:log-algebra and CR.5; the finite logarithm and maximal nilpotence from LefschetzPencilsAndVanishingCycles LPV.1. The analytic log structures are the analytifications of the algebraic ones. Consumer: the optional ordinarity layer of the proposed Part II Reusable infrastructure for potential automorphy over CM fields, Part II: Dwork switching motives.

routes.title: Reusable infrastructure for potential automorphy over CM fields, Part II: polarized automorphy lifting and finiteness of deformation rings
routes.reason: Geraghty's Lemma 5.9 (item 133) is a polarized ordinary local–global statement from Geraghty's ordinary modularity lifting paper, which the proposed Part II PolarizedAutomorphyLifting already draws on for ι-ordinarity and ordinary Hecke algebras. No atlas stage plans it: PotentialAutomorphyInfrastructure PA.2 owns the ordinary tower and the notion of ι-ordinarity, but not the polarized comparison between Galois and automorphic ordinarity. The item joins that proposal under its id, parent, title and area.
routes.brief: Joined proposal. This route joins PolarizedAutomorphyLifting, the Part II of PotentialAutomorphyInfrastructure proposed by the Boxer–Calegari–Gee (2025) extraction and extended by the Newton–Thorne, Clozel–Thorne and other extractions, with the same id, parent, title and area; its brief already covers Geraghty's ordinary modularity lifting with ι-ordinarity and big ordinary Hecke algebras. Qian adds one statement that the proof of Theorem 1.1 uses on p. 1273: Geraghty, Modularity lifting theorems for ordinary Galois representations, Math. Ann. 373 (2019), Lemma 5.9. Let F be an imaginary CM field and π a regular algebraic cuspidal automorphic representation of GL_n(A_F) that is polarizable. If r_{l,ι}(π)|G_{F_v} is ordinary of the corresponding weight (Definition 1.2) at every place v | l, then π is ι-ordinary at every v | l in the sense of Geraghty's Definition 5.3 (item 134, owned by PotentialAutomorphyInfrastructure PA.2). Qian applies it to Sym^{n−1} r_{E_0,l′}|G_{F′}, which is polarizable; Remark 4.4 explains that without polarizability the corresponding local–global statement is not available. Imports: ι-ordinarity from PA.2, the regular ordinary definition from PadicHodgeTheory R06.2, and the Galois representations r_{l,ι}(π) with local–global compatibility from AutomorphicGaloisRepresentationsPartII AG2.4, AG2.5 and AG2.7. Consumer: ModularityAndLanglandsExtensions ML.2 (the proof of Theorem 1.1).

routes.title: Faltings finiteness, semisimplicity and isogeny theorems, Part II: ℓ-adic and residual images of abelian varieties (Serre's open-image theorems)
routes.reason: Serre's open-image theorem for non-CM elliptic curves and the density-zero theorem for their supersingular primes (items 137, 138) have no owner in the atlas: FaltingsFinitenessAndIsogenyTheorems R28.6 explicitly works 'without requiring the full Serre open-image theorem'. The Calegari–Geraghty (2020) extraction proposes this Part II for Serre's open-image theorems, so the two items join it under its id, parent, title and area.
routes.brief: Joined proposal. This route joins OpenImageTheoremsForAbelianVarieties, the Part II of FaltingsFinitenessAndIsogenyTheorems proposed by the Calegari–Geraghty (2020) extraction, with the same id, parent, title and area; its brief already plans Serre's theorem that the ℓ-adic and mod-ℓ images are maximal for large ℓ, for elliptic curves without CM. Qian uses two of Serre's theorems in the proof of Proposition 4.1 (p. 1269) to choose the auxiliary prime l′ and the non-CM elliptic curve E_0/Q: (1) Serre, Propriétés galoisiennes des points d'ordre fini des courbes elliptiques, Invent. Math. 15 (1972): for a non-CM elliptic curve over a number field K, the mod-ℓ representation is surjective onto GL_2(F_ℓ) for all but finitely many ℓ (item 137); (2) Serre, Quelques applications du théorème de densité de Chebotarev, Publ. Math. IHÉS 54 (1981), Théorème 20: the supersingular primes of a non-CM elliptic curve over Q have density zero (item 138), which keeps a positive-density set of primes l′ ≡ 1 mod N at which E_0 is ordinary. ACC+ use the same two theorems in the proof of Corollary 7.2.4 (p. 1100). Imports: the Tate module and Galois representations of elliptic curves from FaltingsFinitenessAndIsogenyTheorems R28.6; Chebotarev from Tau Ceti Chebotarev, Layer 10. Consumer: ModularityAndLanglandsExtensions ML.2 (Proposition 4.1).

gaps.title: Global character roots and Moret–Bailly originals
gaps.detail: Read NSW8.6.7,9.1.6,9.1.9 and the exact Moret–Bailly/CHT4.1.2 variant in their original sources. Decompose local obstruction killing, finite support, restriction/corestriction squares, totally real realization, Galois closure and simultaneous avoidance. The paper's proofs are read but those imported leaves are not closed.
gaps.resolution: Global character roots and Moret–Bailly are cited suppliers.

gaps.title: Fermat, hypergeometric and rank-two source leaves
gaps.detail: Read Deligne's Fermat cohomology §§7.4,7.6,7.10, Beukers–Heckman/Levelt3.5 and the remaining BLGHT4.3/4.7 proofs. Split integral torsion-freeness, analytic/étale lattice comparison, Picard–Lefschetz, residue Hodge calculation and real descent into qualified independent imports. Do not promote a finite-field Gauss identity to a cohomology theorem. The publisher lists an erratum to Deligne's chapter; check it before extracting §7.
gaps.resolution: Fermat, hypergeometric and rank-two inputs are cited suppliers.

gaps.title: Finite transvection and PSL classification

sourceIssues.locator: Lemma 3.12, p. 1267 (statement; proof ends p. 1268). The lemma takes its range of t from the opening of Lemma 3.11, p. 1266: "let t ∈ F_v as a point in T_0(F_v)". Its only use is in the proof of Lemma 4.3, p. 1273.
sourceIssues.printed: "Lemma 3.12 Under the notation and assumption above, and let λ′ be a place of Q(ζ_N) above l′, where l′ ≠ l is an odd prime not dividing N. Then view V_{λ′,t} as a G_{F_v} representation, consider the Weil-Deligne representation WD(V_{λ′,t}) = (r_1, N) associated to it. We have that the operator N is maximally nilpotent."
sourceIssues.correction: Add the hypothesis v(t) < 0. The corrected statement: let v be a place of F above l, and let t ∈ F_v with v(t) < 0 (so t lies in T_0(F_v) and is v-adically close to ∞). Then the monodromy operator of WD(V_{λ′,t}|G_{F_v}) is maximally nilpotent. This is the hypothesis v_K(a) < 0 of Harris–Shepherd-Barron–Taylor, Lemma 1.15, whose argument the proof cites. It also holds wherever the lemma is used: Lemma 4.3 (p. 1273) assumes v(t) < 0 at every l-adic place. With this hypothesis the cited argument works. The restriction of V_{λ′} to the punctured formal neighbourhood of t = ∞ over W(F̄_l) is lisse, because l ∤ N. So inertia at v acts through its tame Z_{l′}-quotient by exp(v(t)·t_{l′}·N_∞), where N_∞ is the logarithm of the monodromy at ∞. That monodromy is maximally unipotent by Corollary 3.5: the loop around t = ∞ is the N-th power of the loop around t′ = ∞, and it is still a single Jordan block. A nonzero multiple of a maximally nilpotent operator in characteristic 0 is again maximally nilpotent, so the corrected statement follows.
sourceIssues.reason: As printed, the lemma covers every t ∈ T_0(F_v), because the only standing condition on t is the one from Lemma 3.11 (p. 1266). The statement is false for t = 0, and more generally for any t ∈ O_{F_v} with t^N − 1 a unit. For such t the hypersurface X_1^N + … + X_N^N = N t X_1⋯X_N has good reduction at v. At a singular point of the reduction the partial derivatives give X_i^N = t X_1⋯X_N for every i, because N is invertible (l ∤ N). Taking the product over i gives (1 − t^N)(X_1⋯X_N)^N = 0, which forces every X_i = 0. The paper uses this same good reduction in Lemma 3.11(2). Since l′ ≠ l, smooth proper base change makes H^{N−2}_et(Y_t ×F̄_v, Z[ζ_N]_{λ′}) unramified at v. Because ζ_N ∈ F, the H_0-action is defined over O_{F_v}, so the χ-eigenspace V_{λ′,t} is also unramified. Hence WD(V_{λ′,t}) has N = 0. But V_{λ′,t} has rank n ≥ 2 (Proposition 3.2, p. 1257), so by Definition 3.6 N = 0 is not maximally nilpotent: its minimal polynomial is X, not X^n. For t = 0 this is completely explicit: V_{λ′,0} is a sum of n characters on which Frobenius acts by Jacobi sums (proof of Lemma 3.9, p. 1262), all unramified at v. A direct check on small Dwork hypersurfaces (N = 3 over F_7 and F_13, N = 5 over F_11) gives singular reduction exactly when t^N ≡ 1. The proof only covers v(t) < 0. It appeals to the monodromy around ∞ and to Harris–Shepherd-Barron–Taylor Lemma 1.15(2), whose statement assumes v_K(a) < 0. Remark 3.13 (p. 1268) also reads the lemma as a statement about v(t) < 0. The recorded correction is right and sufficient. The main theorems are unaffected, because the only application, Lemma 4.3 (p. 1273), has v(t) < 0 at every l-adic place, and there l′ ≡ 1 mod N and l′ > 2ln + 5 (Proposition 4.1, p. 1269). This is an error, not a misprint: a stated lemma is false as printed, not merely mistyped. The intended hypothesis can still be recovered from the context.

sourceIssues.locator: Theorem 1.4, p. 1241, and its proof in the final paragraph of §4 (after Remark 4.4), p. 1274. The cited result is ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2(4): Ann. of Math. 197 (2023), p. 1030, and arXiv:1812.09999v1, p. 109. The v1 numbering (Definition 6.2.28) is the one Qian cites.
sourceIssues.printed: "Let l be an odd prime number." (Theorem 1.4, p. 1241); "all conditions except decomposed genericity follows from the corresponding conditions of r̄" (proof of Theorem 1.4, p. 1274)
sourceIssues.correction: Add the hypothesis l > n to Theorem 1.4. This is the second sentence of condition (4) of ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2; the fourth hypothesis of Theorem 1.4 copies only the first sentence. With l > n added, the proof on p. 1274 works as written. For odd primes l < n with l ∤ n, the paper does not prove Theorem 1.4 (the case l | n is already excluded by the enormity hypothesis). Proving it there would need an ordinary automorphy lifting theorem for such l. Neither ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 nor its later adequate-image version (Miagkov–Thorne, arXiv:2203.04520v2, Theorem 1.3) provides one: both require p > n.
sourceIssues.reason:
**How the proof goes.** On p. 1274, Theorem 1.1 is used to make r̄|G_{F'} ι-ordinarily automorphic, and then ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 is applied at p = l to ρ = r|G_{F'}. The paper says that conditions (3) and (4) of that theorem, apart from decomposed genericity, "follow from the corresponding conditions of r̄".

**The missing condition.** Condition (4) of ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 reads: "There exists σ ∈ G_F − G_F(ζ_p) such that ρ̄(σ) is a scalar. We have p > n." This is the published text on p. 1030, and it is the same in arXiv v1, p. 109. The fourth hypothesis of Theorem 1.4 reproduces the first sentence and drops the second. Nothing in the hypotheses of Theorem 1.4 implies l > n:
- The enormity hypothesis excludes only l | n. ACC+ notes after Definition 6.2.29 that ad⁰ contains the scalars when p | n.
- Enormity puts no lower bound on l in terms of n. For l ∤ n, large subgroups such as SL_n(F_{l^r}) with r large are enormous.
- The other hypotheses (ordinarity, decomposed genericity, the scalar element) do not involve n.

**The bound is needed in ACC+.** The bound p > n is not a removable formality. It is used in the proof of Theorem 6.1.2 in §6.6: at the Ihara-avoidance places, n pairwise distinct characters trivial modulo the uniformiser are chosen, and §6.2.15 on level-raising deformations assumes p > n.

**What is affected.** For odd primes l < n with l ∤ n, Theorem 1.4 is asserted without proof. The first such case is n = 4, l = 3. No counterexample is known, and the statement may well be true there. So this is a gap in the range of a stated result, not a false statement.

**What is not affected.** With l > n added, the published argument proves the theorem. Theorem 1.1 is also unaffected: there ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 is applied at the auxiliary prime l′, which Proposition 4.1 (p. 1269) chooses with l′ > 2ln + 5 > n.

**Defence considered.** The introduction (p. 1241) says Theorem 1.4 is obtained by combining Theorem 1.1 with ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2. One could read that as importing the cited theorem's hypotheses implicitly. This reading does not hold up: Theorem 1.4 lists its hypotheses explicitly, copying conditions (1)–(4) of the cited theorem except for this one sentence, and the proof asserts outright that those conditions follow.

**Version history and later use.** arXiv v1 has the same omission, and there Theorem 1.4 says only "Let l be a prime number". The journal version added "odd" but not l > n. One later paper applies Theorem 1.4 as printed under the sole restriction p ∤ 2n (A'Campo, Rigidity of automorphic Galois representations over CM fields, arXiv:2202.14022v4, Corollary 1.0.5), so it inherits the gap for odd p < n.

sourceIssues.reason: The second condition of Lemma 2.3 (p. 1248) says: when r is even, N ∤ l^{r/2} + 1. The final paragraph of the proof checks this condition. It sets out to prove it ("For the second condition, we need to verify that ..."), and both cases end with the plus sign. If m > 0, then M_1 divides l^{r/2} − 1 and M_1 is an odd divisor of N greater than 1, so "N ∤ l^{r/2} + 1". If m = 0, then N = M_0 = AB and r = 2^{t_0}, and by construction "M_0 = N ∤ l^{2^{t_0−1}} + 1". The target is printed with −1 in both places, and that is not the statement the proof needs. It is true, but it follows at once from the minimality of r, since r/2 < r. So the sign is a misprint. The intended statement is clear from the lemma, from the opening words of the sentence and from the two conclusions that follow, and the argument itself proves the plus-sign version. Neither the lemma nor the proof is affected. A minor point: the caveat "(if t_0 > 0)" is always satisfied, because the construction takes t_0 > 2, so r = 2^{t_0} ∏ p_i^{t_i} is always even. This sentence is not in arXiv v1. There, the proof of this condition simply reads "M_1 | l^{2^{t−1}∏ p_i^{t_i}} − 1 yields a contradiction with N | l^{r/2} + 1" (arXiv v1, p. 9). So the misprint entered when this paragraph was rewritten for publication.

sourceIssues.locator: Section 4, proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.4, the paragraph after Proposition 4.1 beginning "On the side of characteristic l", p. 1270 (arXiv v1, p. 22, same wording, where Lemma 3.9 is numbered 3.8). It restates the third bullet of the choice of N at the start of Section 4, p. 1268.
sourceIssues.printed: We also assumed that F_{l^2} ⊂ k(λ), n | #(k(λ)^×).
sourceIssues.correction: Write n = l^a m with l ∤ m, as the paper does at the start of Section 4 (p. 1268). The sentence should read: "We also assumed that F_{l^2} ⊂ k(λ) and m | #(k(λ)^×)". Equivalently, k(λ) contains all n-th roots of unity in characteristic l, because μ_n(F̄_l) = μ_m. Nothing else changes: the x ↦ x^{l^a} map is a bijection on k(λ)^×, so (k(λ)^×)^n = (k(λ)^×)^m.
sourceIssues.reason: The group k(λ)^× is cyclic of order l^r − 1, which is prime to l. So the printed condition n | #(k(λ)^×) can hold only when l ∤ n. Take n = l = 3: then 3^r − 1 ≡ 2 mod 3 for every r. Theorem 1.1 allows l | n; it has no enormity hypothesis. (In Theorem 1.4 enormity forces l ∤ n, because when l | n the scalars have trace zero, so ad^0 has nonzero invariants.) So as printed, the sentence is false in some cases the theorem covers. It is also not what was assumed. The third bullet on p. 1268 requires F_{l^2}F' ⊂ F_l(ζ_N) = k(λ), where F' is generated by all m-th roots ("hence n-th roots") of elements of F_{l^s}. This gives the two facts the paragraph needs. (i) μ_m ⊂ k(λ). This is exactly the hypothesis of Lemma 2.1 that the finite field contains all n-th roots of unity. The proof of Lemma 2.1 on pp. 1244–1245 writes n = l^a m and uses the exact sequence with kernel Z/mZ, so it needs only this. (ii) Every element of F_{l^s} has an m-th root in k(λ), hence an n-th root in k(λ), since l^a-th powers are a bijection. So det r̄ takes values in (k(λ)^×)^n. The deduction from Lemma 3.9 uses only F_{l^2} ⊂ k(λ). Nowhere else is n | #(k(λ)^×) used; Lemma 3.7 and Proposition 3.8 involve only the order of l mod N. A small case confirms the corrected reading. For n = l = 3 we have m = 1, and the bullet asks for F_9F_{3^s} ⊂ F_3(ζ_N). Cubing is then an automorphism of k(λ)^×, and every k(λ)^×-valued character has a unique cube root. For n = 6, l = 3 the corrected condition 2 | 3^r − 1 always holds, while the printed 6 | 3^r − 1 never does. The intended meaning is clear from the paper's own set-up, and the argument is correct as intended. So this is a misprint (n for its prime-to-l part m) that affects nothing. It is not an error that affects the proof, as the original record said.

sourceIssues.correction: Prove the step from the Frobenius computation inside the proof of Lemma 3.9, not from the statement of the lemma. Let v be a place of F(ζ_N) not dividing Nll′, and let q = #k(v). By (3.1), det V[λ′](Frob_v) = (q^{(N−3)/2} ∏_j g(v,b_j))^n · q^{−n(n−1)/2}. For geometric Frobenius on H^1, det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′}(Frob_v) = q^{n(n−1)/2}. So (det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′})^∨ ⊗ det V[λ′] sends Frob_v to (q^{(N−2n−1)/2} ∏_j g(v,b_j))^n. The exponent (N−2n−1)/2 is an integer because N is odd. By (3.2)–(3.3), ∏_j g(v,b_j) lies in Q(ζ_N) (in Q(ζ_N)^+ when n = 2) and is a unit at λ′, so the base reduces into k(λ′)^× = F_{l′}^×. By Chebotarev, the character takes values in (k(λ′)^×)^n. With the paper's own sign for det Symm^{n−1}, the value is instead (q^{(N−3)/2} ∏_j g(v,b_j))^n, which is also an n-th power. The clause "which have image in F^×_{l^2}" should refer to l′, not l: the character takes values in F_{l′}^×, and for even n those values are in general n-th powers only in F_{l′^2}^×.
sourceIssues.reason: Lemma 3.9 at λ′ gives only det V[λ′](G_F) ⊂ (F_{l′^2}^× k(λ′)^×)^n. Here k(λ′) = F_{l′} because l′ ≡ 1 mod N. On the l side the paper imposed F_{l^2} ⊂ k(λ), but no such condition is available at λ′. Knowing that an element of F_{l′}^× is an n-th power in F_{l′^2}^× does not make it an n-th power in F_{l′}^×. For example, every element of F_{l′}^× is a square in F_{l′^2}. The two determinants also cannot be treated one at a time. Take n even with n | l′−1, as Lemma 2.1 needs. The character χ̄_cyc is onto F_{l′}^× on G_{F(ζ_N)}, because F(ζ_N) is unramified at l′. So there are places v with q a non-square mod l′. At such a v, det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′}(Frob_v) = q^{±n(n−1)/2} is not an n-th power in F_{l′}^×, and so det V[λ′](Frob_v) is not one either. Only their quotient is an n-th power, because the half-integral powers of q cancel as in (3.1). The paper never states this cancellation. sourceIssues.locator: §4, proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.4: Lemma 2.1 is applied at the auxiliary prime λ′ in the paragraph beginning "Now, apply Lemma 2.1" and the paragraph beginning "On the other side of characteristic l′", p. 1270. The hypothesis of Lemma 2.1 is on p. 1244, and the choice of l′ is in Proposition 4.1, p. 1269.
sourceIssues.printed: The condition of Lemma 2.1 is verified below.
sourceIssues.correction:
Add the condition l′ ≡ 1 mod n to Proposition 4.1, so that l′ ≡ 1 mod Nn (N and n are coprime). These primes have Dirichlet density 1/φ(Nn) > 0. The other conditions on l′ exclude only a finite set or a set of density 0, and the fourth condition still follows from the second and third. The later uses of l′ impose no congruence condition that could conflict: the Section 3 hypotheses, Proposition 3.8, and the first paragraph of the proof of ACC+ Corollary 7.2.4. With this condition, k(λ′) = F_{l′} contains μ_n and Lemma 2.1 applies as stated.

Alternatively, the gap closes without any new condition on l′. Put d = gcd(n, l′−1). Then (F_{l′}^×)^n = (F_{l′}^×)^d, and F_{l′} contains μ_d, so Lemma 2.1 with exponent d gives ψ_0 with ψ_0^d = χ. Build an n-th root ψ of χ one primary component of the cyclic group F_{l′}^× at a time:
- if v_p(n) ≤ v_p(l′−1), then n/d is prime to p, and the p-part of ψ is the p-part of ψ_0 raised to an inverse of n/d modulo p^{v_p(l′−1)};
- if v_p(n) > v_p(l′−1), then the p-part of χ is trivial, and so is the p-part of ψ.
Equivalently, the proof of Lemma 2.1 goes through with Z/mZ replaced by μ_n(F_{l^r}), which is cyclic of order gcd(m, l^r−1).
sourceIssues.reason:
Lemma 2.1 (p. 1244) assumes that the finite field F_{l^r} contains all n-th roots of unity. Its proof uses this to identify the kernel of x ↦ x^n on F_{l^r}^× with Z/mZ, where n = l^a m.

In §4 (p. 1270) the lemma is used to produce two characters: χ_1 valued in k(λ)^× and χ_2 valued in k(λ′)^×. For λ the paper states that n | #(k(λ)^×); this comes from the choice of N, up to replacing n by m. For λ′ nothing corresponding is said, and the paragraph on λ′ checks only that the determinant quotient takes values in (k(λ′)^×)^n.

Since l′ ≡ 1 mod N, the prime l′ splits completely in Q(ζ_N), and also in Q(ζ_N)^+ when n = 2, so k(λ′) = F_{l′}. Since l′ > 2ln + 5 > n, F_{l′} contains μ_n exactly when n | l′−1. Proposition 4.1 (p. 1269) imposes only l′ ≡ 1 mod N. Because gcd(N, n) = 1, this says nothing about l′ modulo n. So the hypothesis of Lemma 2.1 is not verified, and it can fail whenever n ≥ 3; for n = 2 it holds automatically.

Small cases:
- n = 3, N = 401 (odd, prime to 3l for l ≠ 401, and greater than 100n + 100). The least prime l′ ≡ 1 mod 401 is 3209, which is 2 mod 3, so F_3209 has no primitive cube root of unity.
- n = 4, N = 503. The least prime l′ ≡ 1 mod 503 is 3019, which is 3 mod 4, so μ_4(F_3019) = {±1}.
In both cases Lemma 2.1 does not apply as stated, but the required root still exists. Cubing is bijective on F_3209^×. In the second case the fourth powers equal the squares, a group of odd order on which the fourth-power map is bijective.

In general the conclusion of Lemma 2.1 holds for every finite field. Both repairs above are valid, and either is sufficient for this point. So this is a missing verification in the proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.4, which share this construction; neither theorem is affected. A separate question is whether the determinant quotient at λ′ really lands in (k(λ′)^×)^n. That is not addressed by this repair and is recorded separately.

sourceIssues.reason:
The page image matches the recorded text exactly, so this is not a text-layer artefact. On p. 1266, v is a place of the number field F above l, and the lemma takes t ∈ F_v as a point of T_0(F_v). So V_{λ,t} is the fibre of the lisse sheaf V_λ at a local point, which makes it a representation of G_{F_v}. It need not come from a representation of G_F.

The rest of the lemma is written locally. The embeddings in (1) are σ : F_v ↪ \overline{ℚ(ζ_N)_λ}, and the hypotheses of (2) and (3) are stated with O_{F_v} and 𝔪_{F_v}. Lemma 3.12, on the same page, explicitly treats V_{λ′,t} as a G_{F_v}-representation. A number field F has no maximal ideal in the sense needed for good reduction, and t ∈ 𝔪_F makes no sense for t ∈ F_v.

The slip comes from a partial change of notation. In arXiv v1 (p. 19), F denotes a finite extension of ℚ(ζ_N)_v, which is a local field. There the corresponding lemma (Lemma 3.10, p. 20) consistently writes G_F, O_F, 𝔪_F and ⊗_{σ,F} B_cris. The published version renamed this local field F_v but did not carry the change through the lemma.

The displayed module in the proof of (3) is the D_{cris,τ} of Remark 2.5. It feeds into Lemma 2.4, which is stated with ⊗_{τ,F_v^0} B_cris, so F_v^0 is the right subscript for the tensor product. The meaning is clear from the statement and the surrounding text, and nothing depends on the slip.

sourceIssues.locator: Section 4, proof of Theorem 1.1, the paragraph after Proposition 4.1 that begins "On the other side of characteristic l′", p. 1270. The same sentence appears unchanged in arXiv v1, p. 22. The representation r̄_{E,l′} is defined in the opening paragraph of Section 4, on p. 1268.
sourceIssues.printed: "we have that det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′} = (χ_cyc)^{n(n−1)/2}, which have image in F_{l′²}^×."
sourceIssues.correction: det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′} = χ̄_cyc^{−n(n−1)/2}, where χ̄_cyc is the mod-l′ cyclotomic character. The paper defines r̄_{E,l′} as H^1_ét(E, F_{l′}) (p. 1268). The printed formula holds instead for the l′-torsion E[l′], that is, for the Tate-module convention. In that convention r_{E,l} is the Tate module and the automorphic object is its dual, as in ACC+, Corollary 7.2.4. The rest of the argument is unchanged, because both characters take values in F_{l′}^× ⊂ F_{l′²}^×.
sourceIssues.reason: By the Weil pairing, ∧²E[l′] ≅ μ_{l′}, so det E[l′] = χ̄_cyc. H^1_ét(E_{Q̄}, F_{l′}) is the F_{l′}-dual of E[l′], so its determinant is χ̄_cyc^{−1}. The same follows from Frobenius eigenvalues. At a prime p ≠ l′ of good reduction, geometric Frobenius acts on H^1 with eigenvalues α, β, where αβ = p. The paper uses χ_cyc in the standard sense (compare the central-character identity on p. 1273), so χ_cyc sends geometric Frobenius to p^{−1}. Now take any 2-dimensional representation whose Frobenius eigenvalues are a and b. The eigenvalues on Symm^{n−1} are a^{n−1−i}b^i for 0 ≤ i ≤ n−1, whose product is (ab)^{n(n−1)/2}. Hence det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′} = χ̄_cyc^{−n(n−1)/2}. The printed identity is false in general. For n = 2 it would say det r̄_{E,l′} = χ̄_cyc, whereas the true determinant is χ̄_cyc^{−1}. These differ by χ̄_cyc², which is nontrivial on G_{F(ζ_N)}: there l′ > 5 and l′ is unramified in F(ζ_N), so χ̄_cyc maps G_{F(ζ_N)} onto F_{l′}^×. The slip is harmless, and its intended meaning is clear. The next sentence uses only that this determinant is a power of the mod-l′ cyclotomic character, so that its values lie in F_{l′}^× ⊂ F_{l′²}^×, and that holds for either sign. Moreover, the two candidates differ by χ̄_cyc^{n(n−1)} = (χ̄_cyc^{n−1})^n, an n-th power. So the n-th-power statement drawn from it with Lemma 3.9 does not depend on the sign. The paper's H^1 convention is itself consistent with the automorphy input in Proposition 4.1: ACC+, Corollary 7.2.4 proves automorphy of the dual of Symm^m of the Tate module, which is Symm^m H^1. The exponent n(n−1)/2 appears to have been carried over from the Tate-module convention; the introduction (p. 1244) also speaks of "the Tate module of an elliptic curve". Since the paper fixes both r̄_{E,l′} and χ_cyc explicitly, the sign is not a matter of convention within the paper.

review.reason: The page image on p. 1257 shows a bar over the whole of W(k)[1/p]. So the paper fixes an isomorphism between ℂ and the algebraic closure of W(k)[1/p], not with W(k)[1/p] itself. Such an isomorphism exists by Steinitz's theorem. Both fields are algebraically closed of characteristic 0, and both have cardinality 2^{ℵ_0}, hence transcendence degree 2^{ℵ_0} over ℚ. This cardinality condition holds when k is finite, or more generally when |k| ≤ 2^{ℵ_0}. The paper does not name k at this point. The companion's blowup lemma (Lemma 2.1 of arXiv:2103.00106v1, pp. 4–5) only needs char k ∤ N, so a finite field of characteristic prime to N can be taken. The base change W(k)[T, U^±] → ℂ[T] needs a ring map from W(k) to ℂ. The paper's map is the composite W(k) ⊂ W(k)[1/p] ⊂ \overline{W(k)[1/p]} ≅ ℂ. This is the same device as the "fixed embedding τ : W → ℂ" in the companion preprint (arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 21). The recorded objection is that W(k)[1/p] is a finite unramified extension of ℚ_p and so is not algebraically closed. That is true, but it concerns a formula the paper does not print. arXiv v1 (p. 13) prints the same formula, with the same bar. There is no misprint here and the proof is unaffected.

sourceIssues.locator: Lemma 4.2 of L. Qian, "Ordinarity of local Galois representation arising from Dwork motives", arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 20. This preprint is reference [14] of the paper and exists only in this version. The paper does not cite Lemma 4.2. It refers only to the main theorem of [14], in Remark 3.13 (p. 1267) and Remark 4.4 (p. 1273). Lemma 3.12 (p. 1266) does not cite [14]. In arXiv v1 of the paper, Lemma 3.10(4) (v1, pp. 20–21) was proved as "the main theorem of [Qia21]". The published version dropped that part.
sourceIssues.printed: "Lemma 4.2. Suppose that F_v is a characteristic 0 local field over ℚ_p and r : Gal(F̄_v/F_v) → GL_n(ℚ̄_p) is semi-stable. Suppose moreover that for every τ : F_v^0 ↪ ℚ̄_p, the operator N on the n-dimensional vector space (r ⊗_{τ,F_v^0} B_st)^{Gal(F̄_v/F_v)} is maximally nilpotent, i.e. the smallest j such that N^j = 0 is n. Then r is regular and ordinary. Proof. This Lemma 2.2 (2) of [BLGHT09]."
sourceIssues.correction:
Add the Hodge–Tate hypothesis of BLGHT Lemma 2.2(2), in shifted form: for every embedding τ : F_v ↪ ℚ̄_p there is an integer k_τ such that the τ-labelled Hodge–Tate weights of r are k_τ, k_τ+1, …, k_τ+n−1, each with multiplicity one. Then r is regular and ordinary.

The case k_τ = 0 is exactly BLGHT Lemma 2.2(2), with conclusion "ordinary of weight 0". The general case follows by twisting by a crystalline character with τ-labelled weight −k_τ; the twist changes neither semistability nor N. It also follows directly from the same weak-admissibility argument.

The proof of the preprint's Theorem 1.1 must then check this hypothesis for V_{λ,t^{-1}}. It holds: the theorem assumes maximally unipotent monodromy at ∞ for every conjugate σχ, and this forces the Hodge numbers of each eigenpart to be 1 in n consecutive degrees.
sourceIssues.reason:
Lemma 4.2 omits a hypothesis of the result it quotes. BLGHT Lemma 2.2(2) also assumes that for every τ the τ-labelled Hodge–Tate weights are exactly 0, 1, …, n−1, each with multiplicity one. Without that hypothesis the statement is false already for n = 2 over ℚ_p.

Counterexample. Let D have basis e1, e2 with φ(e1) = p·e1, φ(e2) = p²·e2, N(e2) = e1 and N(e1) = 0. Then Nφ(e2) = p²·e1 = pφN(e2), so Nφ = pφN. Give D the filtration Fil⁰ = D, Fil¹ = Fil² = Fil³ = ⟨e1+e2⟩, Fil⁴ = 0.
- t_H(D) = 0 + 3 = 3, and t_N(D) = v_p(p·p²) = 3.
- The only nonzero proper N-stable subspace is ker N = ⟨e1⟩. There t_H = 0 ≤ 1 = t_N.
- So D is weakly admissible. By Colmez–Fontaine it is D_st(V) for a 2-dimensional semistable V with Hodge–Tate weights {0, 3} and N ≠ 0, so N is maximally nilpotent and V is regular.
- A G_{ℚ_p}-stable line in V would give a (φ,N)-stable line in D, or a rank-one quotient, with t_H = t_N. The only candidates are ⟨e1⟩ (t_H = 0, t_N = 1) and D/⟨e1⟩ (t_H = 3, t_N = 2).
- Hence V is irreducible and not ordinary, although it satisfies every hypothesis of Lemma 4.2.

Why the weights matter. When N is maximally nilpotent, the only (φ,N)-stable flag is ker N ⊂ ker N² ⊂ …. Because N maps each graded piece isomorphically onto the previous one and Nφ = pφN, the φ-slopes of the graded pieces are s, s+1, …, s+n−1. An ordinary flag needs rank-one admissible pieces, so ordinarity forces the labelled weights to be consecutive. Conversely, if the labelled weights are k_τ, …, k_τ+n−1, then t_H(D) = t_N(D) fixes s. Weak admissibility then forces each ker N^j to carry the lowest j weights at every τ and to be admissible. This gives the ordinary flag.

How far the error reaches.
- The false stated result is Lemma 4.2 itself.
- The preprint's proof of its Theorem 1.1 (pp. 20–23) applies Lemma 4.2 without ever computing Hodge–Tate weights, so that proof has a gap. The gap can be filled. In the limiting mixed Hodge structure at ∞, N has type (−1,−1) and commutes with H_0. Take v in a suitable Deligne component I^{p,q} of the χ-eigenspace. Then v, Nv, …, N^{n−1}v span that eigenspace, so its Hodge numbers are 1 in the n consecutive degrees p, p−1, …, p−n+1. By the de Rham comparison, and because the hypothesis holds for every σχ, these are the labelled Hodge–Tate weights. So Theorem 1.1 itself survives.
- For the family chosen in the paper, the consecutive weights are proved directly in Lemma 3.10(2) and Lemma 3.11(1) (pp. 1265–1266).
- The published paper uses neither Lemma 4.2 nor the main theorem of [14]. It gets ordinarity at l for v(t) < 0 from Lemma 4.3 (p. 1272), through Varma's local-global compatibility and Steinberg local components. Remark 3.13 (p. 1267) says the full strength of the main result of [14] is not needed.
- arXiv v1 of the paper used that main theorem in Lemma 3.10(4), where the consecutive weights were available from Lemma 3.10(1).
- So no stated result of the paper is affected.

sourceIssues.reason:
As printed, Theorems 1.6 and 3.2 are false, so this is an error rather than a gap: the step that fails is the finite-generation claim in (iii). A small case shows this.

Take Y = A^1 over W[T] (so W[T]′ = W[T]), with the log structure pulled back from (W[T], ℕ, 1 ↦ T). Y is strict and smooth over the base, so it is log smooth. Then Ȳ is A^1_W with the chart 1 ↦ 0. For a strict morphism the log differentials are the ordinary ones, so dR_{Ȳ/(W,ℕ,1↦0)} is the complex W[x] → W[x]dx.

Its first cohomology is the direct sum over k ≥ 1 of (W/kW)·x^{k−1}dx. That module is torsion and not finitely generated, so the right-hand side ℍ^1(...)[1/p] is 0.

By step (i) of the proof, which is valid here, the level-n crystalline group is H^1 of W_n[x] → W_n[x]dx, namely the direct sum over k of (W_n/kW_n)·x^{k−1}dx, with surjective transition maps. The classes ξ_n = Σ_{j=1}^{2n} p^{⌊j/2⌋} x^{p^j−1}dx form a compatible system, because the terms with j > 2n vanish mod p^n. For every r, p^r ξ is nonzero at level n = 2r+2: there the coefficient of x^{p^{2r+2}−1}dx is p^{2r+1}, which is nonzero in W/p^{2r+2}. So ξ is not torsion, and the left-hand side (lim_n H^1)[1/p] is nonzero; in fact it is infinite-dimensional. The two sides differ for i = 1.

In general, the limit of (3.6) identifies lim_n ℍ^i(dR_{Ȳ_n}) with an extension of the Tate module of ℍ^{i+1} by the p-adic completion of ℍ^i. This agrees with ℍ^i after inverting p exactly when finiteness holds, and properness supplies finiteness.

The author clearly intended properness: the proof invokes "proper pushforward", and the companion's GAGA statements, Theorem 1.8 (p. 4) and Proposition 3.6 (p. 18), assume it explicitly. But the section states the comparison for an arbitrary log smooth (Y, N), and only "in particular" applies it to the family of Remark 2.4. The stated result therefore has to be restricted. The correction, adding properness, is right. Since the statement as printed has a counterexample, this is an error in a stated result rather than a gap in the proof. Neither version of the main paper uses the comparison outside the proper case.

sourceIssues.correction:
Hypothesis (5) of ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 needs a regular algebraic cuspidal π that is ι-ordinary at every place above the prime, in the sense of Geraghty's Definition 5.3. An automorphic lift that is only ordinary as a Galois representation is not enough. So "ordinarily automorphic" has to be defined on the automorphic side, as in the published Definition 1.3 (p. 1241), and both applications of Theorem 6.1.2 need that input.

(i) The auxiliary prime l′. Sym^{n−1} r_{E,l′}|G_{F′} is polarizable and ordinary above l′, because E has good ordinary reduction at l′. Geraghty's Lemma 5.9 then gives ι′-ordinary automorphy (published, p. 1273).

(ii) V_{λ,t}, which is not polarizable. Prove ι-ordinarity directly, as in the published Lemma 4.3.
- Write V_{λ′,t} ≅ r_{l′,ι′}(π) with ι′ compatible with ι, so that V_{λ,t} ≅ r_{l,ι}(π).
- At each v | l we have v(t) < 0, and Lemma 3.12 shows that WD(V_{λ′,t}|G_{F′_v}) is a single Jordan block.
- Varma's bound WD(r_{l′,ι′}(π)|G_{F′_v})^{F-ss} ≺ ι′^{−1}rec(π_v|det|^{(1−n)/2}) compares partial sums of block sizes, and the two sides have the same semisimplification. So rec(π_v|det|^{(1−n)/2}) is also one block, and π_v ≅ Sp_n(ψ_v|·|^{(1−n)/2}) is a twist of Steinberg.
- The labelled Hodge–Tate weights are consecutive, so the automorphic weight is parallel. Geraghty's ordinarity conditions for this Steinberg representation then scale linearly in j, and they reduce to the single condition at j = n on val_l(ι^{−1}ψ_v(ϖ_v)^n) = val_l(ι^{−1}φ_{π,v}(ϖ_v)).
- That condition is fixed by the continuous, hence unit-valued, l-adic character r_{l,ι}(φ_π) = det r_{l,ι}(π)·ε^{n(n−1)/2}, whose Hodge–Tate weights are nλ_τ.

So V_{λ,t} ⊗ χ_1^{−1} is ι-ordinarily automorphic, and hypothesis (5) holds in the proof of Theorem 1.4. The Galois-side ordinarity taken from the companion preprint (v1 Lemma 3.10(4)) is then no longer needed, and the published version drops it. The conclusions "ordinarily automorphic" in the published Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 are to be read as ι-ordinary automorphy in the sense of the revised Definition 1.3.
sourceIssues.reason:
In arXiv v1, Definition 1.3 (p. 2) calls r̄ ordinarily automorphic when it has an automorphic lift that is "potentially semistable and ordinary with regular Hodge-Tate weights" at every place above l. This is a condition on the Galois side. Under this definition the last sentence of the proof of Theorem 1.1 (p. 24) is correct: Lemma 3.10(4), from the companion preprint, gives Galois ordinarity of V_{λ,t} when v(t) < 0.

The gap is where this Galois-side notion is used in ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2. Hypothesis (5) of that theorem requires π itself to be ι-ordinary in Geraghty's Hecke-theoretic sense. This happens twice:
- On p. 24, for Sym^{n−1} r_{E,l′} ("ordinarily automorphic by our choice of l′").
- On p. 26, for V_{λ,t} ⊗ χ_1^{−1} in the proof of Theorem 1.4, where only conditions (3) and (4) are checked.

Passing from "automorphic and ordinary at l as a Galois representation" to "π is ι-ordinary" is the converse direction of ordinary local–global compatibility. Geraghty's Lemma 5.9 proves it only for polarizable representations. ACC+ Theorem 5.5.1 and Corollary 5.5.2 give only the opposite direction. The Sym^{n−1} case is polarizable, so a citation repairs it. V_{λ,t} is built from a character of H_0 chosen to break self-duality, so it is not known to be polarizable, and it needs a new argument.

The published version identifies exactly this problem in Remark 4.4 (p. 1274), crediting J. Thorne, and supplies Lemma 4.3. I checked Lemma 4.3 against Varma's Definition 1 and Theorem 1 (arXiv:1411.2520):
- A one-block Galois side forces a one-block automorphic side, because (n) is maximal for the order and the semisimplifications agree.
- For a twist of Steinberg with parallel weight, the conditions for 1 ≤ j ≤ n are proportional to j, so only j = n matters.
- The j = n condition says that the normalised central Hecke eigenvalue is an l-adic unit. That follows from r_{l,ι}(φ_π) being a continuous l-adic character.

Small case: n = 2, F′_v = Q_l, λ_τ = 0, the Tate-curve shape. Here r_{l,ι}(φ_π) has Hodge–Tate weight 0, so φ_π has finite order and ψ_v(l)^2 is a unit. Hence π_v = Sp_2(ψ_v|·|^{−1/2}) has a unit U_l-eigenvalue and is ι-ordinary, consistent with the ordinarity of a Tate curve.

The gap therefore affects only proofs. The published version proves Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 in the stronger, automorphic-side sense. Its new restriction to odd l comes from §2 and is unrelated to this point. The phrase "ordinarily automorphic" on its own does not show where the gap is, so the quotation above cites the sentences that invoke Theorem 6.1.2.

A separate bookkeeping remark on Lemma 4.3 (p. 1273), outside this finding: the paper's normalisations are the geometric Artin map and Hodge–Tate weight −1 for the cyclotomic character, as in the proof of Lemma 3.11. With these, a unit-valued l-adic character with labelled Hodge–Tate weights k_τ satisfies val_l(ι^{−1}φ_v(ϖ_v)) = val_l(∏_τ τ(ϖ_v)^{k_τ}). For example, with n = 1, φ = ‖·‖^{−M} and r = ε^{−M}, both sides equal f_v·M. So the exponent −nλ_τ printed there should carry the sign that matches Geraghty's normalisation of the target. Since the same exponent is printed on both sides, the conclusion is unaffected.

sourceIssues.locator: Sentence introducing Theorem 1.4, p. 1241
sourceIssues.printed: Combine our main theorem for residual representation Theorem 1.1 with the automorphy lifting theorem 6.1.2 from [1] and the main result of [14], we obtain a potential automorphy theorem for a single l-adic Galois representation into GL_n.
sourceIssues.correction: Delete "and the main result of [14]". Theorem 1.4 is obtained from Theorem 1.1, or more precisely from its proof (the representation V_{λ,t} ⊗ χ₁⁻¹ built there, which is ι-ordinarily automorphic by Lemma 4.3), together with [1, Theorem 6.1.2] and [1, Lemma 7.1.7]. This is how the last paragraph of §4 argues (p. 1274).
sourceIssues.reason: The page image of p. 1241 shows the sentence exactly as recorded, so this is not a text-layer artefact. The sentence is carried over unchanged from arXiv:2104.09761v1, p. 2, where it cites [Qia21]. In that version the proof of Theorem 1.1 got the ordinarity of V_{λ,t} at the l-adic places from part (4) of the lemma on V_{λ,t} for v(t) < 0, and that part was proved as "the main theorem of [Qia21]". In the published version that part is gone: Lemma 3.11 (p. 1265) has only parts (1)–(3). Its role is taken by Lemma 4.3 (p. 1273), which proves ι-ordinary automorphy from Lemma 3.12, Varma's local-global compatibility [17] and a variant of [8, Lemma 5.6]. The strategy paragraph of the introduction (pp. 1243–1244) was rewritten to match, but this sentence was not. The proof of Theorem 1.4 (p. 1274) uses only the output of the proof of Theorem 1.1, [1, Theorem 6.1.2] and [1, Lemma 7.1.7]. The only result of [14] used anywhere in the published paper is its Lemma 2.1 (a semistable blow-up), in the proof of Lemma 3.3(2) (p. 1257). Remark 3.13 (p. 1268) says the full strength of the main result of [14] is not needed in the paper. Remark 4.4 (p. 1274) goes further and says the argument gives another proof of that main result. So the sentence misdescribes what Theorem 1.4 depends on, but the meaning is clear and no argument is affected. The reported correction is right in substance. I tightened it to say that Theorem 1.4 uses the proof of Theorem 1.1, through Lemma 4.3, and not only its statement.

sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.1, second step (construction of L₁), p. 1248
sourceIssues.printed: We again apply Lemma 4.1.2 of [5] to the extension F₀F₂(μ_{2^r})/ℚ and the set of primes S consisting of p and ∞
sourceIssues.correction: Apply [5, Lemma 4.1.2] to the normal closure over ℚ of F₀F₂(μ_{2^r}), with the same S = {p, ∞} and the same local conditions (E_p/ℚ_p at p, ℝ/ℝ at ∞). This gives a totally real Galois extension L₁/ℚ that is linearly disjoint over ℚ from that normal closure, and hence from each of its subfields. In particular L₁ is linearly disjoint over ℚ from F₂(μ_{2^r}) and from F₀F₂. Only these two disjointness properties are used afterwards. The first shows that F₁ = F₂L₁ and F₂(μ_{2^r}) are linearly disjoint over F₂. The second shows that L₁L₂ and F₀F₂ are linearly disjoint over L₂, so L₁L₂ ∩ F₀ = ℚ. The rest of the proof is unchanged.
sourceIssues.reason:
Clozel–Harris–Taylor, Lemma 4.1.2 (Publ. Math. IHÉS 108, p. 116), assumes that the field D to be avoided is a finite Galois extension of the base, and its proof on p. 117 uses this. For each Galois subextension D_i of D with simple Galois group, it chooses a prime v_i that does not split completely in D_i. The soluble extension E it builds is split at every v_i. Since D and E are both Galois, E ∩ D is Galois with soluble group, so if it were nontrivial it would contain some D_i, which is impossible.

In the first step of the proof of Lemma 2.1 (p. 1245) the lemma is applied to F₀, which is Galois over ℚ, so that step is fine. In the second step (p. 1248) it is applied to F₀F₂(μ_{2^r}), where F₂ = ML₂. Here F₀ and L₂ are Galois over ℚ, but M is an arbitrary CM field: the statement of Lemma 2.1 on p. 1244 does not assume that M is Galois over ℚ, and arXiv:2104.09761v1 only assumes that M is Galois over a CM field F. So F₀F₂(μ_{2^r}) need not be Galois over ℚ. For example, take M = K(i) with K a non-Galois totally real cubic field and F₀ = ℚ. Then F₀F₂(μ_{2^r}) = K·L₂(i, μ_{2^r}) is Galois over ℚ only if it contains the Galois closure of K, and nothing in the construction of L₂ ensures this. So the printed application does not meet the hypothesis of the cited lemma.

Trying to defend the paper: in its only application (p. 1270), Lemma 2.1 is used with M = F(ζ_N) and F₀ = F^avoid F₂^avoid F^suff(ζ_N). This F₀ is Galois over ℚ and contains F(ζ_N), because F^avoid is the normal closure of a field containing F. So there F₀F₂(μ_{2^r}) = F₀L₂(μ_{2^r}) is Galois and the citation is literally valid. The defence therefore saves every use of the lemma in the paper, but not the proof of Lemma 2.1 in the generality stated.

The gap closes at once by passing to the normal closure, because linear disjointness from a field implies linear disjointness from each of its subfields. The later deductions only need the special case of the paper's own second bullet on linear disjointness, applied with D = L₁. So Lemma 2.1 and everything built on it stand, and the kind "gap" and the reach "nothing" are both correctly stated. The wording is identical in arXiv:2104.09761v1, which is the only arXiv version. The published paper is the final version, and no erratum is known.

The original pair satisfies both standing hypotheses of that lemma, because they are hypotheses of Lemma 2.6: r̄(G_F̃) ⊃ SL_2(F_l), and F_1/F is linearly disjoint from F̄^{ker r̄} over F. Also l > 2n + 5 > 2(n − 1) + 3. For n = 1 there is nothing to prove: Symm^0 r̄ is trivial, and any prime p ≠ l that splits completely in F_1 is decomposed generic for it.

The extra hypothesis of part (3) comes from the case being treated. In the reduced setting, H = Ẽ·F̄^{ker ad r̄} is Galois over Ẽ with group ad r̄(G_Ẽ). The normal closure F̃′_s of E_1 over ℚ is also Galois over Ẽ, and H ∩ F̃′_s = Ẽ. So restriction identifies Gal(HF̃′_s/F̃′_s) with Gal(H/Ẽ). That is, ad r̄(G_{F̃′_s}) = ad r̄(G_Ẽ) ⊃ PSL_2(F_l). Since F̃′_s is Galois over ℚ and contains F_1, it contains the normal closure F̃_1 of F_1. Hence ad r̄(G_{F̃_1}) ⊃ PSL_2(F_l), and [1, Lemma 7.1.6(3)] shows that Symm^{n−1} r̄|G_{F_1} is decomposed generic.

Alternatively, keep the reduced pair and note that the proof of [1, Lemma 7.1.6(3)] uses only ad r̄, the hypothesis of (3) and l > 2m + 1. It never uses linear disjointness from F̄^{ker r̄}. The other standing hypothesis, r̄(G_Ẽ) ⊃ SL_2(F_l), does hold for the reduced pair. After the first reduction F is Galois over ℚ, so r̄(G_Ẽ) is normal in r̄(G_F) ⊃ SL_2(F_l) with abelian quotient. Since SL_2(F_l) is perfect for l ≥ 5, it follows that SL_2(F_l) ⊂ r̄(G_Ẽ).
sourceIssues.reason:
[1, Lemma 7.1.6] (Ann. of Math. 197 (2023), p. 1090) has two standing hypotheses on a pair (F, F′). First, r̄(G_F̃) ⊃ SL_2(F_l). Second, F′/F is linearly disjoint over F from F̄^{ker r̄}, the field cut out by r̄ itself. Part (3) adds the hypothesis ad r̄(G_{F̃′}) ⊃ PSL_2(F_l).

The proof of Lemma 2.6(2) makes two reductions "without loss of generality". First it replaces F by F̃ and F_1 by F̃F_1. Then it replaces F by Ẽ and F_1 by E_1 = ẼF_1. It checks only that E_1 is linearly disjoint over Ẽ from H′, and H′ depends only on ad r̄. The quoted sentence then applies [1, Lemma 7.1.6(3)] to the renamed pair (Ẽ, E_1), since F̃′_s is the normal closure of E_1. For that pair, the disjointness of E_1 from Ẽ·F̄^{ker r̄} over Ẽ is neither checked nor true in general.

Example:
- Let F = F_0(ζ_l), where F_0 is a quartic field whose normal closure has Galois group A_4 and is linearly disjoint from ℚ(ζ_l). Then K := F̃ is cyclic cubic over F.
- Let r̄_0 be the restriction to G_F of the mod l representation of an elliptic curve over ℚ with surjective mod l image. Then det r̄_0 = 1 and r̄_0(G_F̃) = SL_2(F_l).
- Let χ : G_F → μ_3 be a cubic character, with fixed field L, that is ramified at a prime of F above a rational prime unramified in H′. This is possible because H′ depends only on ad r̄_0, and such a χ exists by the Grunwald–Wang theorem.
- Put r̄ = r̄_0 ⊗ χ.

Since SL_2(F_l) has no quotient of order 3, Goursat's lemma gives r̄(G_F̃) ⊃ SL_2(F_l). Since det r̄_0 = 1, we get ker r̄ = ker r̄_0 ∩ ker χ, so Gal(F̄^{ker r̄}/F) ≅ SL_2(F_l) × μ_3. Hence L is the only cubic abelian subextension of F̄^{ker r̄}/F. Also L ⊄ H′ ⊇ Ẽ, by ramification.

Let F_1 be one of the two cubic subfields of KL other than K and L. Then F_1/F is Galois. It meets neither F̄^{ker r̄} nor H′; for H′, note that otherwise KF_1 = KL ⊂ H′. So every hypothesis of Lemma 2.6(2) holds. Yet E_1 ⊇ KF_1 = KL ⊇ L, so E_1 ∩ Ẽ·F̄^{ker r̄} ⊇ ẼL ≠ Ẽ. The same failure already occurs after the first reduction.

So the lemma is cited outside its stated hypotheses, in the case that carries all of part (2); the other case ends in a contradiction on p. 1252. The conclusion survives. The original pair satisfies every hypothesis of [1, Lemma 7.1.6], and the extra hypothesis of part (3) follows from H ∩ F̃′_s = Ẽ. Moreover, the proof of part (3) in [1] never uses disjointness from F̄^{ker r̄}.

Lemma 2.6(2) is therefore true as stated. But the printed proof needs this short argument, and the paper does not contain it. This is a gap in the proof, not a false result. The argument in arXiv v1 is the same, citing [1, Lemma 7.1.5(3)] in the older numbering, which has the same standing hypotheses.

sourceIssues.locator: Proposition 3.2, proof, first sentence, p. 1257
sourceIssues.printed: Locally freeness follows because the family is smooth and proper.
sourceIssues.correction:
Smoothness and properness give only that the sheaves are locally constant. For V_λ and V[𝔫] this comes from smooth proper base change, and for V_B and V′_B from Ehresmann's theorem. Because the bases are connected, every stalk is then isomorphic to the stalk at one complex point, using the comparison with V_B stated just before the proposition. Local freeness needs three further facts.
(i) The integral cohomology of a smooth hypersurface Y_t ⊂ ℙ^{N−1} is torsion-free, by the Lefschetz hyperplane theorem and Poincaré duality. So H^{N−2}(Y_t, ℤ[ζ_N]) = H^{N−2}(Y_t, ℤ) ⊗ ℤ[ζ_N] is free. By the universal coefficient theorem, H^{N−2}(Y_t, ℤ[ζ_N]_λ) and H^{N−2}(Y_t, ℤ[ζ_N]/𝔫) are obtained from H^{N−2}(Y_t, ℤ) by tensoring, and they are also free.
(ii) For V_λ and V[𝔫], #H_0 = N^{N−2} is invertible in ℤ[ζ_N]_λ and in ℤ[ζ_N]/𝔫. So the χ-eigenpart is the image of an idempotent. It is a direct summand of a free module over a local ring, or over a finite product of local rings, and is therefore free.
(iii) For V_B and V′_B, N is not inverted. The χ-eigenpart is then a finitely generated submodule of a free module over the Dedekind ring ℤ[ζ_N], hence projective, that is, locally free in the sense of commutative algebra.
In every case the rank equals the dimension over ℚ(ζ_N) of the χ-eigenspace at t = 0. By Deligne's Proposition I.7.4 this dimension is n.
This argument gives only projective stalks for V_B and V′_B, not stalks free over ℤ[ζ_N] itself. The paper uses only their completions at λ and their reductions V_{B,t}/λ and V_{B,t}/𝔫 for λ, 𝔫 prime to 2N, and these are free of rank n.
sourceIssues.reason:
The printed sentence cannot hold as stated. A smooth proper family gives locally constant higher direct images, but their stalks can have torsion: an Enriques surface has H²(X, ℤ) ≅ ℤ^10 ⊕ ℤ/2. So local freeness needs the fibres' integral cohomology to be torsion-free, and it needs the χ-eigenpart to be a direct summand or at least projective. The paper gives neither.
I tried to defend it and the defence fails. The second sentence of the proof checks only the fibre over 0 through Proposition I.7.4 of [7]. That result counts dimensions over a field of characteristic 0 and gives the rank, not freeness. The paper says it adapts the proof of Lemma 4.1 of [4], and that proof does get freeness at t = 0 over ℤ[ζ_N, 1/2N]. But it inverts 2N, so it does not cover V_B or V′_B, whose coefficient ring is ℤ[ζ_N]. Nothing else in the paper supplies torsion-freeness or a direct-summand argument. The companion preprint (arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 2) also asserts local freeness only "by standard comparison results".
The missing facts are standard, so the conclusion is correct. Everything used later concerns localizations or reductions at primes prime to 2N, where the stalks are free of rank n. So the kind is gap, and nothing downstream is affected.

To prove (2), identify V′_B ⊗ ℂ with a hypergeometric local system on ℙ^1 − {0, 1, ∞}. There are two ways to do this:
- as [4] does for its Lemma 4.3(3), by citing Katz (Another look at the Dwork family, Theorem 5.3, together with Exponential sums and differential equations, Theorem 8.4.11);
- through the Picard–Fuchs equation and Levelt's theorem, as in A'Campo (arXiv:2407.16481v1, Lemmas 2.4.5 and 2.5.4 and Proposition 2.5.7).

The second route describes only the pull-back to the t-line, so it determines V′_B only up to a twist by a character ψ of the deck group μ_N. The hypotheses of §3 make n prime to N, so no nonzero translate of {b_1, …, b_n} in ℤ/Nℤ equals the set itself. Hence the hypergeometric system is not isomorphic to any nontrivial twist of itself, its pull-back is irreducible, and the eigenvalues at 0 from part (1) force ψ = 1.

Let e_1, …, e_n be the entries of (a_1, …, a_N) that remain after one copy of each residue that occurs is removed. Then ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) is conjugate to the companion matrix of ∏_k (X − ζ_N^{±e_k}), where a single sign, the same for every k, is fixed by the conventions for characters and loops. For the exponents chosen in §3 the only repeated residue is 0, which occurs n + 1 times. So every e_k = 0, and ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) has characteristic polynomial (X − 1)^n and a single Jordan block. This also gives Corollary 3.5 directly.

The covering t ↦ t′ = t^N is totally ramified over t′ = ∞. A small loop around t = ∞ therefore maps to a conjugate of γ_∞^{±N}, and the pull-back of V′_B is V_B. The blow-up from Lemma 2.1 of [14] and the local monodromy theorem (reduced divisor, e = 1) thus prove only that ρ_{t′}(γ_∞)^N is unipotent, that is, that the eigenvalues of ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) are N-th roots of unity.
