- The proof of (1) applies word for word and gives det ρ_{t′}(γ_0) = ζ_5^{±3} ≠ 1.
- The fibres over μ_N have only ordinary double points, and the fibre dimension N − 2 = 3 is odd. By Picard–Lefschetz, ρ_{t′}(γ_1) is unipotent.
- Since γ_0γ_1γ_∞ = 1, det ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) ≠ 1, so ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) is not unipotent, although the argument of (2) applies to this character word for word.

The same failure occurs for every odd N ≥ 5. Let (a_j) consist of each residue other than −b_1, …, −b_n once, together with n extra entries e_1, …, e_n that avoid the −b_j. Then Σb_j ≡ −Σe_k mod N and det ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) = ζ_N^{±Σe_k}. Any such choice with Σe_k ≢ 0 therefore breaks the argument; an example is b = {1, N − 3} with e = (1, 1).

No reading of the paper rescues the step. The deck-group action on the limit at t = ∞, which would supply the missing eigenvalues in the way part (1) does at t = 0, is never computed. The extra facts (1), (3) and det = 1 do not fix the eigenvalues at ∞ when n ≥ 2. Lemma 3.4 cannot help, because it takes (2) as input.

For the paper's exponents the nonzero entries are distinct and 0 occurs n + 1 times, so every e_k = 0. This is why the statement of Lemma 3.3(2) is still true although its proof fails. A'Campo's Proposition 2.5.7 agrees: on the t-line the monodromy at ∞ is a single unipotent Jordan block. For the counterexample character his parameters give eigenvalues 1 and ζ_5^{±3} at t′ = ∞.

The same step appears in arXiv:2104.09761v1, proof of Lemma 3.3(2), pp. 13–14. Part (2) is used for the eigenvalues at ∞ in Lemma 3.4, and hence in:
- Corollary 3.5;
- the l-power order of the reduction of ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) in the proof of Lemma 3.7 (p. 1259);
- det(γ_∞) = 1 on p. 1260;
- maximal unipotence at ∞ in Lemma 3.12 (p. 1268).
All of these stand once (2) is proved as in the correction. BLGHT's Lemma 4.3(3) had deferred exactly this point to Katz and wished for a direct argument. The printed direct argument does not supply one.

sourceIssues.locator: Lemma 3.3(3), statement p. 1257; proof of (3), p. 1258
sourceIssues.printed: (3) The proof is the same as part 2 of Lemma 4.3 in [4].
sourceIssues.correction:
Keep the Picard–Lefschetz half of the cited argument. The fibre over t′ = 1 has N^{N−2} ordinary double points, and H_0 permutes them simply transitively. So on the χ-part, ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1 has image in the line spanned by the χ-projection of a single vanishing cycle, and rank(ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1) ≤ 1.

Replace the symplectic step with either of the following arguments.

(a) Determinant. By (1), (2) and γ_0γ_1γ_∞ = 1, det ρ_{t′}(γ_1) = ζ_N^{−(b_1+⋯+b_n)}. Moreover b_1+⋯+b_n ≡ a_1+⋯+a_N ≡ 0 mod N, for three reasons:
- {b_1,…,b_n} is the complement of {−a_1,…,−a_N} in ℤ/Nℤ;
- the nonzero a_j are pairwise distinct;
- the elements of ℤ/Nℤ sum to 0 when N is odd.
This agrees with the explicit list of the b_j on p. 1254. Write ρ_{t′}(γ_1) = 1 + v ⊗ f. Then det ρ_{t′}(γ_1) = 1 + f(v) = 1, so f(v) = 0 and (ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1)^2 = f(v)(ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1) = 0. Hence ρ_{t′}(γ_1) is unipotent.

(b) Odd-dimensional Picard–Lefschetz. The fibres have odd dimension N − 2, so the cup product on H^{N−2} is alternating. The vanishing cycles are therefore isotropic, and they are pairwise orthogonal because the double points are distinct. Hence (γ_1 − 1)^2 = 0 on all of H^{N−2} of the fibre, and so also on its χ-part.

Finally, [4] gives only dim ker ≥ n − 1, so the exact equality dim ker(ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1) = n − 1 needs one more step. If ρ_{t′}(γ_1) = 1, then ρ_{t′}(γ_0) = ρ_{t′}(γ_∞)^{−1} would be unipotent. This contradicts (1), because no b_j is 0 in ℤ/Nℤ.
sourceIssues.reason:
The proof of [4, Lemma 4.3(2)] has two steps.
- Picard–Lefschetz theory shows that ker(γ_1 − 1) has rank at least n − 1. This part carries over unchanged to the family Y′ with the character χ.
- Unipotence then follows from the sentence "As γ_1 acts as a symplectic transformation we conclude that it has characteristic polynomial (X − 1)^n". This works in [4] because the χ-part there becomes, after extending scalars, the sheaf Ṽ_B, which carries a perfect alternating pairing, and ρ̃ takes values in Sp_n. In effect the step uses det = 1.

Neither step can be replaced by a symplectic structure in the present setting. The cup product pairs the χ-part of H^{N−2} only with the χ^{−1}-part. Also χ^2 ≠ 1 on H_0: since N is odd, χ^2 = 1 would force all the a_j to be congruent mod N, but the a_j take both values 0 and 1. Symplecticity of γ_1 on the whole of H^{N−2} constrains only the pair of χ- and χ^{−1}-parts, and gives no information on det ρ_{t′}(γ_1). There is no alternative self-pairing either. Lemma 3.1 with α = −1 gives {−b_j} ≠ {b_j}, so the eigenvalues of ρ_{t′}(γ_0) are not closed under inversion. Hence the monodromy on V′_B, which is irreducible because no b_j is 0, preserves no nonzero bilinear form. Avoiding such self-duality is the stated purpose of the choice of the a_j (p. 1255). So the step the "same" proof relies on is not available.

I also looked for another reading and found none. The paper never computes det ρ_{t′}(γ_1), and it never uses the odd-dimensional form of the Picard–Lefschetz formula. Lemma 3.4 shows ρ(γ_1) = BA^{−1} with corner entry C_n, but C_n is not identified with 1. The remark det(γ_1) = 1 on p. 1260 is stated after the lemma and without proof. The needed facts are easy to supply: I checked that b_1 + ⋯ + b_n ≡ 0 mod N from the printed a_j for all n from 3 to 29 and many admissible N, and this also matches the printed list of the b_j. So the statement of Lemma 3.3(3) is correct and only its proof is incomplete.

Unipotence is really used later:
- Lemma 3.7 needs the residual image to be generated by transvections, which is the hypothesis of the classification theorem in [18].
- p. 1260 uses det(γ_1) = 1.
Lemma 3.4 and the irreducibility argument after Definition 3.6 need only rank(ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1) = 1.

sourceIssues.locator: Lemma 3.7, p. 1259: the first assertion (about ρ̄_{t′}) in the case n = 2, and the first sentence of the proof. The relevant definitions are Y′ and V′_B on p. 1256 and the n = 2 convention on p. 1257.

Alternatively, keep the n = 2 case of the first assertion but state explicitly that for n = 2 the symbols T′_0 and V′_B denote the family Ỹ → T̃_0 of [4] and its sheaf Ṽ_B. In that family t̃^{−1} multiplies the middle term X̃_{(N+1)/2}^N, whose exponent in χ is 0. [4, Lemma 4.6] is a statement about Ṽ_B.
sourceIssues.reason:
The definition on p. 1256 holds for every n ≥ 2. It sets Y′ : X′_1^N + ⋯ + X′_{N−1}^N + t′^{−1}X′_N^N = N X′_1⋯X′_N and V′_B = (R^{N−2}π̃′_*ℤ[ζ_N])^{χ,H_0}. The n = 2 convention on p. 1257 replaces only V_λ, V[𝔫] and V_B by the sheaves of [4]. It does not replace V′_B.

The paper identifies the two families by X′_N = tX_N and t′ = t^N. Under this identification, the deck transformation t ↦ ζ_N t of T_0 − {0} → T′_0 acts on Y − Y_0 as the element ξ = (1, …, 1, ζ_N^{−1}) of H. Transport the action to the Fermat fibre over t = 0. There ρ_{t′}(γ_0) acts on the χ_i-line by ζ_N^{±(a_N+i)}, for i ∈ {b_1, …, b_n}.

For n > 2 the character on p. 1253 has a_N = 0, which gives Lemma 3.3(1). For n = 2 it has a_N = N − 1, and {b_1, b_2} = {(N−1)/2, (N+1)/2} (p. 1254). The eigenvalues of ρ_{t′}(γ_0) are then ζ_N^{±(N−3)/2} and ζ_N^{±(N−1)/2}. So det ρ_{t′}(γ_0) = ζ_N^{∓2}, which is a primitive N-th root of unity because N is odd. Since l ∤ N, it remains ≠ 1 modulo λ. Hence for n = 2 the image of ρ̄_{t′} does not lie in SL, and the first assertion is false for the sheaf the paper defines.

There is an equivalent way to see this. In [4, §4] the family Ỹ over T̃_0 = T′_0 lets t̃^{−1} multiply the middle coordinate, where χ has exponent 0. The two deck elements differ by (1, …, ζ_N, …, 1, ζ_N^{−1}) ∈ H_0, with ζ_N in position (N+1)/2. On this element χ takes the value ζ_N^{0−(N−1)} = ζ_N. So for n = 2 the paper's V′_B is the sheaf Ũ_B of [4] twisted by a character of order N that factors through the deck group. In particular V′_B ⊗ ℚ has no ℚ(ζ_N)^+-form: the eigenvalues ζ_N^{(N+1)/2} and ζ_N^{(N+3)/2} of γ_0 are not stable under complex conjugation. Yet p. 1258 takes λ to be a prime of ℤ[ζ_N]^+ when n = 2. The cited [4, Lemma 4.6] concerns Ṽ_B, not this sheaf.

The best defence is to read V′_B for n = 2 silently as Ṽ_B of [4]. The citation of [4] and the choice of λ in ℤ[ζ_N]^+ point that way, and under that reading the lemma is true. However, it is not what pp. 1256–1257 define, so the defence fails on the text as written. The defect is notational in origin, but the printed statement is false.

The damage is limited to the statement of Lemma 3.7. For n = 2 the second assertion is [4, Corollary 4.7], as p. 1257 notes. Proposition 3.8 (p. 1261) uses only that second assertion, and no later argument uses ρ̄_{t′} for n = 2.

The arXiv version has the same wording and definitions (the lemma is numbered 3.6 there).

sourceIssues.locator: Lemma 3.9, proof, case n = 2: the sentence introducing (3.3), which begins on p. 1263 and ends on p. 1264
sourceIssues.printed: For this, it suffices to take a σ ∈ G_{ℚ_l(ζ_N)^+} such that σ(ζ_N) = ζ_N^{−1} and σ(ζ_p) = ζ_p
sourceIssues.correction: Drop the condition σ(ζ_p) = ζ_p. Take any σ ∈ G_{ℚ_l(ζ_N)^+} with σ(ζ_N) = ζ_N^{−1} (such a σ exists exactly when ℚ_l(ζ_N)^+ ≠ ℚ_l(ζ_N); otherwise (3.2) already gives the claim), and write σ(ζ_p) = ζ_p^c. The substitution used for (3.2) gives σ(g(v,b)) = t(c^{(q−1)/N})^{−b} g(v,−b). The prefactors cancel in the product because b_1 + b_2 ≡ 0 mod N, and {−b_1, −b_2} = {b_1, b_2}, so σ fixes g(v,b_1)g(v,b_2). More directly: for n = 2, b_1 = (N−1)/2 and b_2 = (N+1)/2 ≡ −b_1 mod N, so the identity g(v,a)g(v,−a) = q displayed on p. 1263 (N odd, a ≠ 0) gives g(v,b_1)g(v,b_2) = q ∈ ℚ. A third route treats the Gauss sums as algebraic numbers in ℚ(ζ_N, ζ_p) and uses Gal(ℚ(ζ_N, ζ_p)/ℚ(ζ_N)^+). There a σ with σ(ζ_N) = ζ_N^{−1} and σ(ζ_p) = ζ_p does exist, because ℚ(ζ_N) and ℚ(ζ_p) are linearly disjoint over ℚ (p ∤ N).
sourceIssues.reason:
The step fails under the paper's own conventions. The additive character ψ takes values in the p-th roots of unity in Q̄_l (p. 1262). The primes l and p are distinct and prime to N, so ℚ_l(ζ_N, ζ_p) is unramified over ℚ_l. Every σ ∈ G_{ℚ_l} therefore acts on it as a Frobenius power Frob_l^m (m ∈ Ẑ), sending ζ_N to ζ_N^{l^m} and ζ_p to ζ_p^{l^m}.

Let r be the order of l mod N. An element of G_{ℚ_l(ζ_N)^+} sending ζ_N to ζ_N^{−1} exists only when −1 is a power of l mod N, that is, when l^{r/2} ≡ −1 mod N; it then has m ≡ r/2 mod r. The extra condition σ(ζ_p) = ζ_p requires m ≡ 0 modulo the order s of l mod p. Both hold for some m exactly when gcd(r, s) divides r/2, i.e. when v_2(s) < v_2(r). This fails for a positive proportion of primes p.

Two concrete cases satisfy the §3 hypotheses for n = 2 (p. 1259: l an odd prime, N odd and prime to 2l, N > 300):
- N = 307, l = 613 = 2N − 1, p = 5. Here l ≡ −1 mod N forces m to be odd, while 613 ≡ 3 mod 5 has order 4, which forces 4 | m.
- N = 301, l = 3, p = 5. Here 3 has order 42 mod 301 and 3^{21} ≡ −1 mod 301, so m ≡ 21 mod 42 is odd, while 3 has order 4 mod 5.

A direct search of the relevant finite cyclic Galois groups confirms that no σ exists in either case. So (3.3) as printed is not established for the places v above such p. The second line of (3.3) uses σ(ζ_p) = ζ_p essentially, since it leaves ψ(x) unchanged.

When −1 is not a power of l mod N, ℚ_l(ζ_N)^+ = ℚ_l(ζ_N). Then no element of G_{ℚ_l(ζ_N)^+} sends ζ_N to ζ_N^{−1}, so the requested σ does not exist either, but the n = 2 claim is already (3.2).

Defences considered:
- Reading ℚ_l as ℚ throughout the passage would make every step correct (third route). But the paper uses ℚ_l(ζ_N) consistently, in (3.2) and in the statement to be shown, together with Q̄_l-valued ψ, so this is not a slip in one symbol.
- The conclusion does follow from the identity g(v,a)g(v,−a) = q printed a few lines earlier, since b_2 = −b_1. The paper never draws this conclusion, however; it rests the n = 2 case on the nonexistent σ.

Hence the step is wrong but locally repairable. The asserted membership is true, since the product equals q. A numerical check of g(v,(N−1)/2)g(v,(N+1)/2) = q for (N, q) = (11, 23), (15, 31) and (307, 1229) agrees.

Reach: Lemma 3.9 stands, and so do the main results. At both primes where §4 applies the lemma, −1 is not a power of the prime mod N: l satisfies N ∤ l^{r/2} + 1 (p. 1268), and l′ ≡ 1 mod N (Proposition 4.1). There ℚ_l(ζ_N)^+ = ℚ_l(ζ_N), so (3.2) suffices. arXiv:2104.09761v1, p. 18, has the same sentence.

sourceIssues.locator: Remark 3.13, p. 1268
sourceIssues.printed: We remark that the proof of the main theorem of [14] shows that when v(t) < 0, V_{λ,t} (as a G_{F_v} representation) is semistable whose associated Weil-Deligne representation also has a maximally nilpotent operator N.
sourceIssues.correction: Claim only what the proof in [14] gives. Take t ∈ F_v with v(t) = −d < 0 and write t^{−1} = uπ^d, where u is a unit and π is a uniformiser. Then V_{λ,t} is potentially semistable. It becomes semistable on restriction to G_{F′}, where F′ = F_v(π^{1/e}) is the totally ramified extension of [14, Theorem 1.4]. The integer e comes from a toroidal subdivision and is not controlled. The rest of the sentence holds as printed: the monodromy operator N of WD(V_{λ,t}) can be computed from D_st over F′, and it is maximally nilpotent. The argument of [14] gives semistability over F_v itself only when v(t) = −1. In that case the blow-up of [14, Lemma 2.1], base-changed along T ↦ t^{−1}, is already a semistable model of Y_t over O_{F_v}. For v(t) ≤ −2 the claim needs a separate argument. One option is a semistable model of Y_t over O_{F_v}; this means gluing compatible semistable resolutions of the local models uπ^d = Z_1⋯Z_r. Another is to combine two facts: ℓ′-adic inertia acts unipotently on the whole middle cohomology, as in the proof of Lemma 3.12, and the traces of inertia on D_pst do not depend on ℓ, by Ochiai's theorem.
sourceIssues.reason:
The remark cites the proof of the main theorem of [14]. That proof works throughout over an auxiliary ramified extension:
- Theorem 1.4 and Theorem 2.3 of [14] (arXiv:2103.00106v1, pp. 3 and 9) give a semistable model of the Dwork hypersurface only over O_{F′}, where F′ = F(π^{1/e}).
- The integer e comes from the subdivision theorem of Kempf, Knudsen, Mumford and Saint-Donat (pp. 11–12), and it is never shown to be 1.
- Only the case of valuation −1 is settled over F itself (p. 8, after Remark 2.2). The same page notes that the naive base change for d ≥ 2 has local form uπ^d = Z_1⋯Z_r, which is not semistable.
- Section 4 of [14] (p. 19) reduces at the start to proving that V_{λ,t^{−1}} is regular and ordinary as a G_{F′}-representation. The operator N is then computed on D_st over F′, using Tsuji's comparison theorem for the model over O_{F′} (pp. 20–21).
- Lemma 4.1 of [14] descends from F′ to F only the properties de Rham, regular and ordinary, never semistability.
- The main theorem of [14] is itself stated for an arbitrary finite extension F_0, and its proof replaces F_0 by F′.

1. Read "semistable" as "potentially semistable". This would make the sentence correct, but the paper keeps the two notions apart: its Theorem 1.4 (p. 1241) requires r|_{G_{F_v}} to be "potentially semistable". The remark also offers its claim as the p-adic analogue of the unipotent ℓ′-adic inertia of Lemma 3.12, which points to genuine semistability. So the missing word is not a plain misprint.
2. Look for the claim elsewhere in the paper. Nothing supplies it. Remark 4.4 proves only ordinarity, via local–global compatibility, and ordinarity in the sense of [1] does not imply semistability over F_v.

The statement about N is correct. The Weil–Deligne representation of a potentially semistable representation can be computed from D_st over any extension over which it becomes semistable. F′/F_v is totally ramified, so the maximal unramified subfield is unchanged, and [14] shows N is maximally nilpotent on each embedding component. The semistability claim is plausible, but the cited proof does not establish it.

Nothing depends on the remark. It says itself that the result of [14] is not needed. The main proof uses the ℓ′-adic Lemma 3.12, through Lemma 4.3, and Remark 4.4 refers back to Remark 3.13 only for ordinarity. The remark does not appear in arXiv v1. There, Lemma 3.10(4) cited [14] only for "regular and ordinary". The published paper is the final version, and arXiv has no later version of either paper.

The first step can kill the finitely many nonzero local classes of all factors at once, using the least common multiple of their orders. The graded pieces form a lattice in V_{λ,t}^{ss}, and its reduction is isomorphic to V[λ]_t ≅ χ̄_1 ⊗ r̄|G_{F′} because V[λ]_t is semisimple.

So the printed sentence claims in particular that G_{F′} acts semisimply on V_{λ,t}. Lemma 4.3 and Remark 4.4 use the sentence in exactly this form.

The only way to pass from λ′ to λ is to compare Frobenius characteristic polynomials and then apply Chebotarev and Brauer–Nesbitt. That identifies only V_{λ,t}^{ss} with r_{l,ι}(π). Semisimplicity of the Galois action on the étale cohomology of the fibre Y_t is not known.

(ii) V_{λ′,t} is irreducible because its reduction χ̄_2 ⊗ Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′}|G_{F′} is absolutely irreducible. But irreducibility of r_{l,ι}(π) is not known for a non-polarizable π over a CM field, and irreducibility is not known to be independent of the prime.

This follows from the Lefschetz trace formula applied to Frobenius composed with elements of H_0: H_0 acts trivially on the cohomology of Y_t outside the middle degree (weak Lefschetz and Poincaré duality), and χ is nontrivial.
Second, ι and ι′ must induce the same embedding of ℚ(ζ_N). Lemma 4.3 needs this as well, since its proof uses a single π for both primes, via r_{l′,ι′}(π).

Here ι′ is chosen so that ι′ (through λ′) and ι (through λ) induce the same complex embedding of ℚ(ζ_N). The comparison follows from the equality of Frobenius characteristic polynomials across the compatible system, together with Chebotarev and Brauer–Nesbitt, because r_{l′,ι′}(π) is semisimple.

Replace the sentence by the following argument, which needs no new hypothesis.

2. The semisimplified Weil–Deligne representation depends only on the semisimplification of the Galois representation. So WD(r_{l′,ι′}(π)|G_{F′_v})^{ss} is the same segment.
3. By Varma's Theorem (1ss), which applies because v ∤ l′, the same holds for ι′^{−1}rec_{F′_v}(π_v|det|_v^{(1−n)/2})^{ss}. Hence the cuspidal support of π_v|det|_v^{(1−n)/2} is a single segment of n characters.

By Zelevinsky's classification, a generic irreducible representation is an irreducible product δ(Δ_1) × ⋯ × δ(Δ_k) of essentially square-integrable representations whose segments are pairwise unlinked. Splitting one segment into k ≥ 2 pieces always produces two juxtaposed pieces, which are linked. So k = 1.

Alternatively, at the one place where the lemma is applied, in the proof of Theorem 1.1 (pp. 1272–1273), V_{λ′,t} is irreducible. Attempts to defend the paper:
- V_{λ,t} ≅ r_{l,ι}(π) does not imply irreducibility of r_{l,ι}(π). The non-polarizable case is exactly the setting of the paper.
- Monodromy density for the family gives irreducibility only for generic t, not for every t with v(t) < 0.
- The gap is filled only at the lemma's application in the proof of Theorem 1.1. There the residual representation of V_{λ′,t} ⊗ χ̃_2^{−1} is stated on p. 1272 to be absolutely irreducible, and Theorem 6.1.2 of ACC+ even gives V_{λ′,t} ≅ r_{ι′}(π′) directly.

The lemma remains true as stated, by the repair above. Its ingredients are:
- Lemma 3.12, which gives the Weil-group semisimplification as a single segment;
- Varma's semisimplified compatibility at v ∤ l′;
- Shalika's genericity of the local components of a cuspidal π;
- Zelevinsky's classification of generic representations, which forces the twisted Steinberg representation.

The remainder of the proof uses only V_{λ,t} ≅ r_{l,ι}(π), the Hodge–Tate weights of Lemma 3.11 and the central character, so it is unchanged. Lemma 4.3 and Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 are therefore unaffected; only the written proof needs repair.

sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Lemma 4.3, second paragraph, p. 1273
sourceIssues.printed: “we see that the weight of the automorphic representation π must be of form (−λ_τ)_τ, here in terms of Geraghty's notation it means that all λ_{τ,i} = −λ_τ for a fixed τ. … it suffices to show that val_l(ι^{−1}(ψ_v(det(α^{(n)}_{ϖ_v})))) = val_l(∏_{τ:F′_v↪Q̄_l} τ(ϖ_v)^{−nλ_τ}) … Thus r_{l,ι}(φ_π) is an l-adic character of Hodge-Tate weight (nλ_τ)_τ, and since the image of r_{l,ι}(φ_π) are all l-adic units, we see that val_l(ι^{−1}(φ_{π,v}(ϖ_v))) = val_l(∏_{τ:F′_v↪Q̄_l} τ(ϖ_v)^{−nλ_τ}) and we are done.”
sourceIssues.correction: In the conventions the paper uses, π has weight (λ_τ)_τ, that is, λ_{τ,i} = +λ_τ for all i. Both the identity to be shown and the identity obtained should read val_l(ι^{−1}φ_{π,v}(ϖ_v)) = val_l(∏_{τ:F′_v↪Q̄_l} τ(ϖ_v)^{nλ_τ}), where ψ_v(det α^{(n)}_{ϖ_v}) = ψ_v(ϖ_v)^n = φ_{π,v}(ϖ_v). For general j the condition is val_l(ι^{−1}ψ_v(ϖ_v)^j) = val_l(∏_τ τ(ϖ_v)^{jλ_τ}). Once both signs are corrected, dividing by n and multiplying by j works as before, the argument closes, and Lemma 4.3 holds.
sourceIssues.reason:
The page image of p. 1273 matches the quoted text. The paper uses the conventions of Allen et al. [1], Ann. of Math. 197 (2023):
- Art sends uniformizers to geometric Frobenius (p. 906), and HT_τ(ε) = {−1} (p. 907).
- For π of weight λ, HT_τ(r_ι(π)) = {λ_{τ,1}+n−1, …, λ_{τ,n}} ([1, Theorem 6.1.1(5)(b), p. 1029]).
- For the central character, HT_τ(r_ι(ω_π)) = Σ_i λ_{τ,i} and det r_ι(π) = r_ι(ω_π)ε^{n(1−n)/2} ([1, p. 987]).

The paper's Lemma 2.4 (p. 1250) and Definition 1.2 (p. 1240) use the same normalisation. The proof of Lemma 3.11 (pp. 1266–1267) uses it too: there V_{λ,0} ≅ ⊕_i Q̄_l(−M(a_τ)−i) on inertia, with weights {M, …, M+n−1}, and Lemma 3.11(3) gives the ordinary weight λ_{τ,i} = M(a_τ). So consecutive weights {λ_τ, …, λ_τ+n−1} mean λ_{τ,i} = +λ_τ.

The proof itself uses this convention. It computes the weight of r_{l,ι}(φ_π) = det r_{l,ι}(π)·χ_cyc^{n(n−1)/2} as nλ_τ, which requires HT(χ_cyc) = −1; with the opposite sign it would get nλ_τ + n(n−1). By [1, p. 987], weight nλ_τ also forces Σ_i λ_{τ,i} = nλ_τ, not −nλ_τ.

The last step has the wrong sign. Let φ be an algebraic Hecke character and let h_τ be the τ-weight of r_{l,ι}(φ). On F′_v^×, r_{l,ι}(φ)∘Art_v = ι^{−1}φ_v·∏_τ τ(·)^{a_τ}. Near 1 the character φ_v is trivial and ε∘Art_v(u) = N(u), which gives a_τ = −h_τ. The left side takes unit values, so evaluating at ϖ_v gives val_l(ι^{−1}φ_v(ϖ_v)) = val_l(∏_τ τ(ϖ_v)^{+h_τ}). As a check, take φ = ||·||: then r_{l,ι}(φ) = ε, and val_l(q_v^{−1}) = −f_v = val_l(∏_τ τ(ϖ_v)^{−1}), whereas the printed rule gives +f_v.

The target identity has the same wrong sign. Suppose Geraghty labels weights dually, so that "(−λ_τ)" is literally correct in his notation. The target still cannot be right. At j = n the normalised operator is central, so its condition holds either for every π of these Hodge–Tate weights or for none, and ι-ordinary ones exist. Also, [1, Corollary 5.5.2, p. 1028] and Matsumoto (arXiv:2312.01551v3, Lemma 4.34(2), pp. 46–47, from Geraghty's proofs of Lemmas 5.4 and 5.7) apply Geraghty's Definition 5.3 to π of weight λ in the sense of [1] without any change. Matsumoto's criterion requires val_l(ι^{−1}χ_i(ϖ_v)) = e_v^{−1}Σ_τ(λ_{τ,n+1−i}+i−1+(1−n)/2). The constituents of Sp_n(ψ_v|·|^{(1−n)/2}) are ψ_v|·|^s for s = (1−n)/2, …, (n−1)/2, and for parallel weight the criterion reduces to val_l(ι^{−1}ψ_v(ϖ_v)) = val_l(∏_τ τ(ϖ_v)^{λ_τ}).

Both printed identities are false whenever Σ_{τ|v} λ_τ ≠ 0, which happens here: for n = 2, λ_τ = M(a_τ) = (N−3)/2 > 0. The two sign errors cancel, so Lemma 4.3 is unaffected. The passage does not appear in arXiv v1.

sourceIssues.locator: Remark 4.4, p. 1274
sourceIssues.printed: “Hence by the main local-global compatibility result Theorem 5.5.1 or [1], we see that V_{λ,t} as a G_{F′_v} representation is ordinary for any l-adic places v of F. … the attempt of deducing V_{λ,t} being ι-ordinarily automorphic from the fact that it is automorphic and ordinary as l′-adic representation seems invalid”
sourceIssues.correction: Read “Theorem 5.5.1 of [1]” (whose form for a single ι-ordinary automorphic representation is [1, Corollary 5.5.2]), “for any l-adic place v of F′”, and “ordinary as l-adic representation”, meaning ordinary at the l-adic places of F′.
sourceIssues.reason: There are three slips. First, the paper has no Theorem 5.5.1; in [1] Theorem 5.5.1 is the local–global compatibility theorem for ordinary parts, so “or” should be “of”. Second, the remark restricts V_{λ,t} to G_{F′_v}, so v must be a place of F′; the paper states the same assertion with “any l-adic place of F′” on p. 1243 and in Lemma 4.3 on p. 1273. Third, V_{λ,t} is the λ-adic realisation with λ above l, so it is an l-adic representation. The superseded argument, at the end of the proof of Theorem 1.1 in arXiv:2104.09761v1 (p. 24), deduced ordinary automorphy from V_{λ,t} being automorphic and ordinary at the l-adic places when v(t) < 0 (arXiv:2104.09761v1, Lemma 3.10(4), the main theorem of [14]). The published paper also uses ordinarity of V_{λ′,t} at the l′-adic places (v(t) > 0 there), but only to make V_{λ′,t} automorphic through the lifting theorem; it says nothing about π at the l-adic places. The “local-global compatibility result in this direction” that needs polarizability goes from Galois ordinarity to ι-ordinarity at the same prime, and the paper applies it in that form ([8, Lemma 5.9]) to Sym^{n−1} r_{E,l′} on p. 1273. So the remark makes sense only with “l-adic”. The remark is not used in any proof.

sourceIssues.locator: Remark 4.4, p. 1274
sourceIssues.printed: Hence by the main local-global compatibility result Theorem 5.5.1 or [1], we see that V_{λ,t} as a G_{F′_v} representation is ordinary for any l-adic places v of F. This gives another way of proving the main result of [14].
sourceIssues.correction: First fix the misprints: "Theorem 5.5.1 or [1]" should read "of [1]", and "l-adic places v of F" should read "of F′". Then make the deduction only when the residual representation V[λ]_t ≅ χ̄_1 ⊗ r̄|G_{F′} of V_{λ,t} is absolutely irreducible and decomposed generic. Twisting by a character preserves both properties, so this is the same as asking that r̄|G_{F′} be absolutely irreducible and decomposed generic. That holds in the setting of Theorem 1.4, but not in general in Theorem 1.1. Under this condition, cite the single-representation result [1, Corollary 5.5.2], or equivalently [1, Theorem 5.5.1] together with [1, Lemma 6.2.11] after the soluble base change used in that corollary's proof. The conclusion then covers only the global points t produced in the proof, and only on the decomposition groups of F′ at places above l. For those points it gives the conclusion of the main theorem of [14]. It does not give it for every t of negative valuation over every finite extension of an l-adic field containing ζ_N.
sourceIssues.reason:
[1, Theorem 5.5.1] is stated on p. 991 and restated on pp. 1026–1027 of the Annals version. It concerns Galois representations valued in ordinary Hecke algebras. It carries the standing hypothesis that F contains an imaginary quadratic field in which l splits, and it assumes [F^+:ℚ] > 1, a non-Eisenstein maximal ideal (by Definition 2.3.6, an absolutely irreducible residual representation) and a decomposed generic residual representation. The version for a single automorphic representation is [1, Corollary 5.5.2] on p. 1028. It requires the residual representation to be decomposed generic and irreducible. That corollary was added at a referee's request and appears first in the June 2022 arXiv revision; it is not in the December 2018 version that the paper cites.

The remark presents its conclusion as a consequence of the proof of Theorem 1.1, where r̄ is only semisimple. For a reducible r̄, or one that is not decomposed generic, the residual representation χ̄_1 ⊗ r̄|G_{F′} fails these hypotheses. A polarized local–global result such as Geraghty's cannot replace them, because V_{λ,t} is deliberately not self-dual. Irreducibility also matters for a second step. Transfer from the auxiliary prime l′ gives only V_{λ,t}^{ss} ≅ r_{l,ι}(π), and ordinarity of the semisimplification does not imply ordinarity of V_{λ,t}, because the order of the characters in the ordinary flag is prescribed. An absolutely irreducible residual representation makes V_{λ,t} irreducible and so closes this step.

Defence: in the setting of Theorem 1.4 the remark is correct. The proof of that theorem on p. 1274 shows that r̄|G_{F′} is absolutely irreducible, using linear disjointness from F^{avoid}, and decomposed generic, using [1, Lemma 7.1.7]. The remark, however, is not restricted to that setting.

The phrase "another way of proving the main result of [14]" overstates what is shown. [14, Theorem 1.1] (arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 2) proves ordinarity for every t of negative valuation over every finite extension of a local field containing ζ_N. The remark covers only the global points given by Moret-Bailly's theorem.

The remark is not used anywhere. [1, Theorem 6.1.2(5)] (p. 1030) needs π to be ι-ordinary, which Lemma 4.3 supplies, and does not need Galois ordinarity of r_ι(π).

sourceIssues.locator: Companion preprint (Qian, Ordinarity of local Galois representation arising from Dwork motives), proof of Lemma 2.1, regularity of U_k, arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 6
sourceIssues.printed: If all of the coefficients are 0, we see that a_j = 0, ∀j < k from f_j = 0 since l ∤ N.
sourceIssues.correction: … from f_j = 0 since char(k) ∤ N.
sourceIssues.reason: The page image confirms the sentence is printed as recorded, so this is not a text-layer artefact. The l is a math-italic l, the same glyph as the index function l(x) of p. 5, and ∤ is typeset correctly. For j < k the variable x_j does not occur in the product ∏_{l(k)≤s≤N, s≠i} x_s, so f_j = ∂f/∂x_j = −N a_j^{N−1}. The step f_j = 0 ⇒ a_j = 0 therefore needs N to be a unit in k̄: the point q is a k̄-point, and the Jacobian is read in m/m² ⊗_{k(m)} k̄. That condition is char(k) ∤ N, which is the standing hypothesis of §2 ("In this section we always assume char(k) ∤ N and N > 1", arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 4). It also follows from the assumption on p. 1 that the residue characteristic p of F does not divide N, since k is the residue field of F. Here char(k) means the residue field k, not the index k that appears in the same sentence. The companion never introduces a prime l. On p. 5 the letter denotes the index function l(x). Its only other use is the phrase "the l-adic representation V_{λ,(uπ)^{-1}}" on p. 8, where it loosely stands for the residue characteristic of λ, and by p. 1 that is p = char(k). Under either reading the intended hypothesis is char(k) ∤ N, so the meaning is clear and the argument is unaffected. There is no later version of the companion: arXiv has only v1. The published paper (Invent. Math. 231 (2023)) cites the companion only as a 2021 preprint and does not reproduce this argument; it only invokes Lemma 2.1 on p. 1257.

On p. 23, replace "the punctured unit disc" by S ∖ {0}. Over this S the map π^an : Y^an → S is proper and log smooth, so [Ill94] 2.2.2 and 2.2.3 apply. For every s ∈ S ∖ {0} the condition (s^{de}u′)^N ≠ 1 then holds automatically. Under t = 1/(τ(u′)T^{de}), a loop around T = 0 in S ∖ {0} goes to a loop in the region |t| > 1 that winds de times around t = ∞. So the identification of the monodromy with ρ_s(γ_∞)^{de} goes through. Nothing else changes, because the argument only uses a neighbourhood of T = 0. Alternatively, take u′ in Remark 2.4 to be the Teichmüller lift [ū] of ū, which Remark 2.4 allows because any lift of ū will do. Then τ(u′) is a root of unity, all excluded points lie on the unit circle, and the open unit disc can be kept as printed.
sourceIssues.reason:
The printed sentence matches the page image. By Remark 2.4 (p. 13), Y is defined only over Spec W[T]′, the open subscheme of Spec W[T] where (T^{de}u′)^N ≠ 1. Here u′ ∈ W^× is any lift of the reduction ū of u. The scheme Y is a blow-up of u′T^{de}(X_1^N + ⋯ + X_N^N) = N X_1⋯X_N that is an isomorphism away from T = 0.

The removed fibres really are singular. For λ ≠ 0, the hypersurface λ(X_1^N + ⋯ + X_N^N) = N X_1⋯X_N is singular exactly when λ^N = 1. At a singular point the partial derivatives force λX_i^N = X_1⋯X_N for every i, and taking the product of these equations gives λ^N = 1. Conversely, if λ^N = 1, a point with every X_i ∈ μ_N and X_1⋯X_N = λ is singular. After base change along the embedding τ : W → ℂ fixed on p. 21, the excluded points are therefore the de·N values of T with (T^{de}τ(u′))^N = 1. All of them have absolute value |τ(u′)|^{−1/(de)}.

Nothing forces this radius to be at least 1. For example, u′ = [ū](1 + p) is an admissible lift. Since τ([ū]) is a root of unity and τ(1 + p) = 1 + p, we get |τ(u′)| = 1 + p for every τ. The excluded points then lie on the circle of radius (1 + p)^{−1/(de)} < 1, strictly inside the printed unit disc. For such a u′, Y^an is not defined over all of S and π^an is not proper over S, so [Ill94] 2.2.2 cannot be applied with S the unit disc. The condition (s^{de}u′)^N ≠ 1 on p. 23 shows that these points were not excluded from S.

The monodromy step on p. 23 fails in the same way. Take a base point s beyond the excluded circle. A loop around 0 through s is carried by t = 1/(τ(u′)T^{de}) into the region |t| < 1 around t = 0. Its monodromy is then a power of the monodromy around t = 0, not ρ_s(γ_∞)^{de}.

The missing restriction on the disc, or on the choice of u′, is always available, and the argument is local at T = 0. So this is a gap, not an error, and Theorem 1.1 of the companion is unaffected. However, the step as printed is invalid for some admissible choices of u′, so the proof needs the amendment above. The reach is therefore the proof, not nothing. The published main paper does not depend on this passage beyond the stated theorem. Its own Lemma 3.3(2) (published p. 1257) specialises U ↦ 1 and works over 𝔸^1 ∖ μ_N, where the excluded points lie on the unit circle, so that separate argument is not affected.
